MATHEMATICS Addition combines quantities. Subtraction finds a

solving an equation, keep both sides balanced by doing the same valid
operation to each side.

matter are solid, liquid, and gas. Melting changes a solid into a
liquid. Freezing changes a liquid into a solid. Evaporation changes a

attracts objects with mass. Friction resists motion between surfaces.

BIOLOGY Cells are the basic units of life. The heart pumps blood around

processes information and helps control the body. The digestive system
breaks food down so nutrients can be absorbed. DNA stores hereditary
information. Plants use photosynthesis to convert light energy into
stored chemical energy. An ecosystem includes organisms and their
physical environment. Producers make food, consumers eat other
organisms, and decomposers break down dead material.

EARTH AND SPACE Earth is the third planet from the Sun. The eight
planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and
Neptune. The Sun is a star. The Moon orbits Earth. Earth rotates,
causing day and night. Earth’s tilt and orbit cause the seasons. The
Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean. Weather describes short-term
atmospheric conditions. Climate describes long-term weather patterns.
The water cycle includes evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.

COMPUTERS AND AI Hardware is the physical part of a computer. Software
is the set of programs and instructions. The CPU executes instructions.
RAM temporarily stores data currently in use. A variable stores a value
in a program. A function is reusable code that performs a task. A loop
repeats instructions. An algorithm is a sequence of steps for solving a
problem. A database stores organized information. Machine learning uses
data to train models to recognize patterns or produce outputs. A dataset
is a collection of examples. Training data helps a model learn.
Validation data helps evaluate and tune a model. Test data measures
performance on examples not used for training. Overfitting happens when
a model learns training examples too specifically and performs poorly on
new examples. A lower training loss does not automatically mean an AI is
more intelligent. Good AI training requires accurate data, suitable
methods, and careful evaluation.

GEOGRAPHY AND GENERAL KNOWLEDGE Canada is in North America. Ottawa is
the capital of Canada. Canada has ten provinces and three territories.
Toronto is the capital of Ontario. The Canadian dollar is Canada’s
currency. The five commonly recognized oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic,
Indian, Southern, and Arctic. A map represents a geographic area.
Latitude measures position north or south of the Equator. Longitude
measures position east or west of the Prime Meridian.

DAVIDAI GENERAL KNOWLEDGE AND CONVERSATION DATASET Version 1.0 Purpose:
A broad starter text corpus for learning language patterns, facts,
explanations, reasoning, and helpful conversation. Important: This is
educational training text, not a complete or always-current
encyclopedia. Facts can change. DavidAI should learn to say when it is
unsure, ask clarifying questions, and avoid inventing facts.

============================================================ SECTION 1 —
CONVERSATION AND COMMUNICATION
============================================================

User: Hello. DavidAI: Hello! How can I help you today?

User: Hi, how are you? DavidAI: I’m doing well and ready to help. How
are you?

User: Good morning. DavidAI: Good morning! What would you like to work
on?

User: Good night. DavidAI: Good night! I hope you have a restful
evening.

User: Thank you. DavidAI: You’re welcome! I’m glad I could help.

User: Thanks a lot. DavidAI: You’re very welcome.

User: Please. DavidAI: Of course. What do you need?

User: Sorry. DavidAI: That’s okay. What would you like to do next?

User: Goodbye. DavidAI: Goodbye! Have a great day.

User: What is your name? DavidAI: My name is DavidAI.

User: Who made you? DavidAI: I am DavidAI, an AI project created by my
developer. I should not claim to know details that have not been
provided to me.

User: What can you do? DavidAI: I can answer questions, explain
concepts, help with writing, brainstorm ideas, solve suitable problems,
and assist with learning. My abilities depend on the tools and knowledge
available to me.

User: Do you know everything? DavidAI: No. I have limits and can make
mistakes. If I do not know something, I should say so rather than make
up an answer.

User: I don’t understand. DavidAI: No problem. I can explain it in
simpler words, give an example, or break it into smaller steps.

User: Explain that again. DavidAI: Certainly. I will try a different
explanation and make each step clearer.

User: That answer is wrong. DavidAI: Thanks for pointing that out.
Please show me which part is wrong or provide the correction. I should
check the information and update my understanding when appropriate.

User: You made a mistake. DavidAI: I may have. Let’s inspect the
reasoning and correct the error instead of defending an incorrect
answer.

User: Can you be shorter? DavidAI: Yes. I will keep the answer concise.

User: Can you explain in more detail? DavidAI: Yes. I will add context,
examples, and a step-by-step explanation.

User: Tell me a joke. DavidAI: Why did the computer go to the doctor? It
had a virus!

User: I am bored. DavidAI: We could explore an interesting science fact,
invent a story, solve a puzzle, or brainstorm a project.

User: I have an idea. DavidAI: Great! Tell me about it. I can help you
develop it.

============================================================ SECTION 2 —
LANGUAGE, GRAMMAR, AND WRITING
============================================================

Language is a system people use to communicate meaning. It can be
spoken, written, signed, or communicated through other shared symbols.

A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. Examples include teacher,
Ottawa, bicycle, and courage. A verb describes an action or state.
Examples include run, think, build, and be. An adjective describes a
noun. Examples include blue, enormous, careful, and interesting. An
adverb often describes a verb, adjective, or another adverb. Examples
include quickly, very, and carefully. A pronoun can replace a noun.
Examples include I, you, she, they, and it. A preposition shows a
relationship, often involving place, time, or direction. Examples
include in, under, before, and toward. A conjunction connects words,
phrases, or clauses. Examples include and, but, because, and although.
An interjection expresses a short reaction. Examples include oh, wow,
and ouch.

A sentence normally contains a subject and a predicate. The subject
tells what or whom the sentence is about. The predicate tells something
about the subject. Example: The small dog chased the ball. Subject: The
small dog. Predicate: chased the ball.

A statement gives information: The library closes at six. A question
asks for information: When does the library close? A command gives an
instruction: Please close the door. An exclamation expresses strong
feeling: What a wonderful discovery!

A paragraph develops one main idea. A useful paragraph often begins with
a topic sentence, follows with supporting details, and ends with a
concluding sentence.

A summary presents the most important ideas in fewer words. A good
summary keeps the original meaning and does not add unsupported claims.
A paraphrase expresses an idea in new wording while preserving its
meaning. A quotation repeats another source’s exact words and should be
clearly identified.

Common punctuation: A period ends a statement. A question mark ends a
direct question. An exclamation mark shows strong emotion or emphasis. A
comma separates items or helps organize a sentence. An apostrophe can
show possession or a contraction. Quotation marks identify direct speech
or quoted words. A colon can introduce a list or explanation. A
semicolon can connect closely related independent clauses.

Examples of contractions: I am becomes I’m. You are becomes you’re. They
are becomes they’re. Do not becomes don’t. Cannot becomes can’t. It is
becomes it’s. Its, without an apostrophe, usually shows possession.

Commonly confused words: There refers to a place or introduces a
statement. Their shows that something belongs to them. They’re means
they are. Your shows possession. You’re means you are. Its shows
possession. It’s means it is or it has. To can show direction or form an
infinitive. Too can mean also or excessively. Two is the number 2. Then
usually relates to time or sequence. Than is used in comparisons. Affect
is usually a verb meaning to influence. Effect is usually a noun meaning
a result.

Verb tenses: Present: I walk to school. Past: I walked to school.
Future: I will walk to school. Present continuous: I am walking. Past
continuous: I was walking. Present perfect: I have walked. Past perfect:
I had walked.

Adjectives can be compared: Positive: tall. Comparative: taller.
Superlative: tallest. Some adjectives use more and most: more careful,
most careful.

Good writing is clear, organized, accurate, and appropriate for its
audience. Prefer specific words over vague words. Use examples when they
make an explanation easier to understand. Revise writing for meaning
before correcting small punctuation details.

============================================================ SECTION 3 —
MATHEMATICS ============================================================

Mathematics studies numbers, quantities, patterns, shapes, structures,
and change.

Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. Integers include negative whole
numbers, zero, and positive whole numbers. Fractions represent parts of
a whole. In 3/4, 3 is the numerator and 4 is the denominator. Decimals
use place value based on powers of ten. Percent means per hundred.
Therefore, 25% = 25/100 = 0.25 = 1/4.

Place value: In 4,582, the 4 represents four thousands, the 5 represents
five hundreds, the 8 represents eight tens, and the 2 represents two
ones. A digit’s value depends on its position.

Addition combines quantities. Subtraction finds a difference or removes
a quantity. Multiplication can represent repeated addition or equal
groups. Division splits a quantity into equal groups or finds how many
groups fit.

Example: 7 × 8 = 56. Example: 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Example: 145 + 278 = 423.
Example: 500 − 186 = 314.

Order of operations: 1. Parentheses and other grouping symbols. 2.
Exponents. 3. Multiplication and division, working from left to right.
4. Addition and subtraction, working from left to right. Example: 3 + 4
× 2 = 3 + 8 = 11, not 14.

A factor divides a number evenly. A multiple is the result of
multiplying a number by an integer. Prime numbers have exactly two
positive factors: 1 and themselves. Examples of primes include 2, 3, 5,
7, 11, and 13. The number 1 is not prime. A composite number has more
than two positive factors.

Fractions: To add fractions with the same denominator, add the
numerators and keep the denominator. Example: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. To add
fractions with different denominators, find a common denominator.
Example: 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. To multiply fractions, multiply
the numerators and multiply the denominators. Example: 2/3 × 3/5 = 6/15
= 2/5. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Example: 1/2
÷ 1/4 = 1/2 × 4/1 = 2.

Decimals: 0.5 = 1/2. 0.25 = 1/4. 0.75 = 3/4. 0.1 = 1/10. When adding
decimals, line up the decimal points. When multiplying by 10, 100, or
1000, place value shifts accordingly.

Percentages: 10% of 80 = 8. 25% of 80 = 20. 50% of 80 = 40. To find a
percentage, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. If 18 out
of 20 questions are correct, the percentage is 18 ÷ 20 × 100 = 90%.

Ratios compare quantities. A ratio of 2:3 means two parts of one
quantity for every three parts of another. Equivalent ratios can be made
by multiplying or dividing both terms by the same nonzero number.

Algebra uses symbols to represent numbers. A variable is a symbol, often
a letter, whose value may be unknown or may change. An expression
combines numbers, variables, and operations. An equation states that two
expressions are equal. Example: x + 5 = 12. Subtract 5 from both sides:
x = 7. Example: 3x = 21. Divide both sides by 3: x = 7. The goal when
solving an equation is to keep both sides balanced by performing the
same valid operation on both sides.

Geometry: A point identifies a location. A line extends infinitely in
both directions. A line segment has two endpoints. An angle is formed by
two rays with a common endpoint. An acute angle is less than 90 degrees.
A right angle is exactly 90 degrees. An obtuse angle is greater than 90
degrees and less than 180 degrees. A straight angle is 180 degrees. A
triangle has three sides and three angles. The interior angles of a
triangle add to 180 degrees. A quadrilateral has four sides. The
interior angles of a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees.

Perimeter is the distance around a two-dimensional shape. Area measures
the surface inside a two-dimensional shape. Rectangle perimeter = 2 ×
(length + width). Rectangle area = length × width. Square area = side ×
side. Triangle area = (base × height) ÷ 2. Circle circumference = 2πr.
Circle area = πr². The radius is the distance from the center of a
circle to its edge. The diameter is twice the radius.

Volume measures space occupied by a three-dimensional object.
Rectangular prism volume = length × width × height. Cube volume = side³.
Surface area is the total area of the outside faces of a
three-dimensional object.

Statistics: Mean is the arithmetic average: add all values and divide by
the number of values. Median is the middle value after sorting the data.
Mode is the most frequent value. Range is the maximum minus the minimum.
A graph communicates data visually. A bar graph compares categories. A
line graph often shows change over time. A pie chart shows parts of a
whole.

Probability measures how likely an event is. Probability ranges from 0
to 1, or from 0% to 100%. An impossible event has probability 0. A
certain event has probability 1. For equally likely outcomes,
probability = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.

============================================================ SECTION 4 —
PHYSICS AND EVERYDAY SCIENCE
============================================================

Science is a systematic way of investigating the natural world through
observation, questions, experiments, evidence, and explanations.

A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation or prediction. A
variable is something that can change in an investigation. The
independent variable is the factor deliberately changed. The dependent
variable is the factor measured. Controlled variables are kept the same
to make a fair test. A conclusion explains what the results show and
whether they support the hypothesis.

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Common states of
matter are solid, liquid, and gas. Plasma is another state found in
stars and some electrical phenomena. Solids usually keep their shape and
volume. Liquids keep a volume but take the shape of their container.
Gases spread out to fill their container. Heating often increases
particle motion. Cooling often decreases particle motion. Melting
changes a solid into a liquid. Freezing changes a liquid into a solid.
Evaporation changes a liquid into a gas at its surface. Boiling occurs
throughout a liquid at its boiling point under a given pressure.
Condensation changes a gas into a liquid. Sublimation changes a solid
directly into a gas.

Mass measures the amount of matter in an object. Weight is the force of
gravity acting on an object’s mass. Mass is commonly measured in
kilograms. Weight is a force and is commonly measured in newtons.
Density = mass ÷ volume. An object less dense than a fluid may float in
that fluid, depending on the overall forces and conditions.

A force is a push or pull that can change an object’s motion or shape.
The SI unit of force is the newton. Gravity attracts objects with mass
toward one another. Friction resists relative motion between surfaces.
Air resistance is a type of drag caused by moving through air. A
balanced set of forces produces no acceleration. An unbalanced net force
causes acceleration.

Speed = distance ÷ time. Velocity includes both speed and direction.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. An object can accelerate
by speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. Newton’s first law
describes inertia: an object maintains its state of rest or uniform
straight-line motion unless acted on by a net external force. Newton’s
second law is commonly written F = ma, where force equals mass times
acceleration. Newton’s third law states that interacting objects exert
equal and opposite forces on each other.

Energy is the capacity to cause change or do work. Kinetic energy is
energy of motion. Gravitational potential energy depends on position in
a gravitational field. Thermal energy is related to the microscopic
motion and interactions of particles. Chemical energy is stored in
chemical arrangements. Electrical energy is associated with electric
charges and fields. Energy can be transferred and transformed. In
ordinary physical processes, total energy is conserved, although useful
energy may become spread out as thermal energy.

A simple electric circuit needs a conducting path and an energy source.
A closed circuit allows current to flow. Current is the rate of flow of
electric charge and is measured in amperes. Voltage is electric
potential difference and is measured in volts. Resistance is measured in
ohms. Ohm’s law for many simple resistive components is V = IR. A
conductor allows electric charge to move relatively easily. An insulator
resists charge movement. Never experiment with household mains
electricity. Electrical learning projects should use safe, low-voltage
equipment and adult supervision where appropriate.

Sound is a mechanical wave that travels through a medium such as air,
water, or a solid. Sound cannot travel through a perfect vacuum.
Frequency is measured in hertz and relates to perceived pitch. Amplitude
relates to wave strength and often to loudness. Light is electromagnetic
radiation. Visible light is the portion detectable by human eyes. Light
travels much faster than sound in air. Reflection occurs when light
bounces from a surface. Refraction is a change in direction caused by a
change in wave speed between materials. A prism can separate white light
into a spectrum of colors.

Heat naturally transfers from warmer regions to cooler regions.
Conduction transfers thermal energy through direct interactions.
Convection transfers thermal energy through the movement of fluids.
Radiation transfers energy through electromagnetic waves and does not
require a material medium.

============================================================ SECTION 5 —
CHEMISTRY ============================================================

Chemistry studies matter, its properties, its composition, and how it
changes. An atom is a basic unit of a chemical element. Atoms contain
protons, neutrons, and electrons. Protons have positive electric charge.
Neutrons have no electric charge. Electrons have negative electric
charge. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. The atomic number
equals the number of protons in an atom’s nucleus. An element is defined
by its number of protons.

A molecule is a group of atoms bonded together. A compound contains
atoms of two or more different elements chemically combined. A mixture
contains substances physically combined rather than chemically bonded
into one pure substance. Water is H2O: each molecule contains two
hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Carbon dioxide is CO2. Oxygen gas is
commonly O2. Common table salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.

The periodic table organizes chemical elements by atomic number and
recurring properties. Rows are called periods. Columns are called
groups. Elements in the same group often have similar chemical
properties. Metals are generally good conductors and are often shiny and
malleable. Nonmetals have varied properties and are often poor
conductors. Metalloids have some properties of metals and some of
nonmetals.

A physical change changes form or state without making a new substance.
A chemical change forms one or more new substances. Evidence of a
chemical reaction may include a color change, gas production, a
temperature change, light, or formation of a solid precipitate. No
single observation always proves a chemical reaction by itself.

The pH scale is commonly used to describe how acidic or basic an aqueous
solution is. A pH below 7 is acidic. A pH of 7 is neutral at standard
reference conditions. A pH above 7 is basic or alkaline. The exact pH
interpretation depends on temperature and the solution.

A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction. A balanced chemical
equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides. Matter
is conserved in ordinary chemical reactions. For example, 2H2 + O2 →
2H2O represents hydrogen reacting with oxygen to form water. Chemical
substances should never be tasted or mixed casually. Follow laboratory
safety rules and use adult supervision in educational experiments.

============================================================ SECTION 6 —
BIOLOGY AND THE HUMAN BODY
============================================================

Biology is the study of living things. Living organisms are made of one
or more cells. A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of
life. Many cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, and genetic material.
The nucleus of many eukaryotic cells contains most of the cell’s DNA.
Mitochondria help release usable energy from food molecules through
cellular respiration. Ribosomes build proteins. Plant cells usually have
a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole. Chloroplasts
carry out photosynthesis.

Photosynthesis uses light energy to help convert carbon dioxide and
water into sugars, releasing oxygen as a by-product. A simplified
equation is: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen.
Plants also carry out cellular respiration to release energy from
sugars.

The human body has many interacting systems. The skeletal system
supports the body and protects organs. The muscular system helps produce
movement and maintain posture. The nervous system sends and processes
signals. The circulatory system moves blood, oxygen, nutrients, and
waste products. The respiratory system exchanges oxygen and carbon
dioxide. The digestive system breaks food into substances the body can
absorb. The urinary system helps remove wastes and regulate water and
salts. The immune system helps defend the body against pathogens.

The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood. Arteries carry blood
away from the heart. Veins carry blood toward the heart. Capillaries are
tiny vessels where substances are exchanged with surrounding tissues.
Red blood cells carry oxygen using hemoglobin. White blood cells help
defend against infection. Platelets help blood clot.

The lungs contain branching airways ending in tiny air sacs called
alveoli. Gas exchange occurs across the thin surfaces of the alveoli and
nearby capillaries. The diaphragm is an important muscle used in
breathing.

Digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing breaks food into smaller
pieces and saliva begins chemical digestion. The stomach mixes food with
acid and enzymes. The small intestine is a major site of nutrient
digestion and absorption. The large intestine absorbs water and helps
form solid waste.

DNA stores hereditary information. Genes are sections of DNA that
contribute to inherited traits and biological functions. Chromosomes are
structures made of DNA and proteins. Different versions of a gene are
called alleles. Inherited traits are influenced by genes and often by
environmental factors as well.

An ecosystem includes living organisms and their physical environment. A
producer, such as a green plant, makes organic food using energy from
sunlight or chemical sources. A consumer obtains energy by eating other
organisms. A decomposer breaks down dead material and waste, recycling
nutrients. A food chain shows one pathway of energy transfer. A food web
connects many food chains. Energy flows through ecosystems, while matter
such as nutrients is recycled.

Biodiversity means the variety of life at genetic, species, and
ecosystem levels. Adaptation is an inherited feature that can improve
survival or reproduction in a particular environment. Natural selection
occurs when inherited variations affect reproductive success across
generations. Evolution is change in populations over generations.

============================================================ SECTION 7 —
EARTH AND SPACE SCIENCE
============================================================

Earth has several major layers: crust, mantle, outer core, and inner
core. The crust is the thin, solid outer layer. The mantle is a thick
layer of hot rock that can flow very slowly over geological time. The
outer core is liquid and composed mainly of iron and nickel. The inner
core is solid, largely because of immense pressure.

Tectonic plates are large pieces of Earth’s lithosphere that move
slowly. Plate boundaries can be associated with earthquakes, volcanoes,
mountain building, and seafloor spreading. An earthquake is the shaking
of the ground caused by a sudden release of energy in Earth’s crust or
lithosphere. A volcano is an opening through which molten rock, gases,
and other materials can reach the surface. Weathering breaks down rocks.
Erosion transports sediment. Deposition occurs when transported material
is dropped.

The water cycle describes the movement of water through Earth’s systems.
Evaporation changes liquid water into water vapor. Transpiration
releases water vapor from plants. Condensation forms tiny liquid
droplets or ice crystals in the atmosphere. Precipitation includes rain,
snow, sleet, and hail. Runoff flows over land into streams, rivers,
lakes, and oceans. Infiltration allows water to enter the ground.

Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions. Climate describes
long-term patterns of weather in a region. Temperature, air pressure,
humidity, wind, and precipitation are important weather variables.
Clouds form when moist air cools and water vapor condenses or deposits
onto tiny particles. Wind is air moving from areas of higher pressure
toward areas of lower pressure, influenced by Earth’s rotation and other
factors.

The solar system contains the Sun, planets, dwarf planets, moons,
asteroids, comets, and other objects. The Sun is a star at the center of
our solar system. Earth is the third planet from the Sun. The eight
planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter,
Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. The inner planets are rocky. Jupiter and
Saturn are gas giants. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. A moon is a
natural satellite orbiting a planet or another smaller body.

Earth rotates once approximately every 24 hours, producing the daily
cycle of day and night. Earth orbits the Sun once approximately every
365.25 days. Earth’s axial tilt, together with its orbit, causes the
seasons. The Moon orbits Earth. The phases of the Moon occur because we
see different portions of its sunlit half as it moves around Earth. A
solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun. A
lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon.

A light-year is a unit of distance, not time. It is the distance light
travels in one year. A galaxy is a large collection of stars, gas, dust,
and dark matter held together by gravity. The Milky Way is the galaxy
containing our solar system. Stars produce energy through nuclear fusion
in their cores. The observable universe contains an enormous number of
galaxies.

============================================================ SECTION 8 —
COMPUTERS AND PROGRAMMING
============================================================

A computer is a machine that processes information according to
instructions. Hardware means the physical parts of a computer. Software
means programs and instructions that run on hardware. The central
processing unit (CPU) executes instructions. Random access memory (RAM)
temporarily stores data and programs in active use. Storage devices keep
data even when power is off. A graphics processing unit (GPU) is
designed to handle many parallel calculations, especially graphics and
other workloads. An operating system manages hardware and provides
services for applications.

A bit is a binary digit: 0 or 1. A byte is commonly eight bits. Binary
uses base 2. Decimal uses base 10. Hexadecimal uses base 16. Computers
represent many kinds of information using patterns of bits.

An algorithm is a defined sequence of steps for solving a problem or
completing a task. A program is a set of instructions written in a
programming language. A bug is an error or defect in a program.
Debugging is the process of finding and fixing bugs. A variable stores a
value that a program can use or change. A function is a reusable block
of code that performs a task. A parameter is an input a function
receives. A loop repeats instructions. A conditional chooses behavior
based on whether a condition is true or false. A data structure
organizes information, such as a list, array, map, or tree.

Programming languages include Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, C,
C++, C#, and Rust. HTML describes the structure of web pages. CSS
controls presentation and layout. JavaScript adds behavior and
interactivity to web pages. TypeScript adds a type system to JavaScript.
Python is often used for automation, education, data analysis, and
machine learning.

Example Python: def greet(name): return “Hello,” + name + “!”

print(greet(“Alex”))

A web browser requests and displays web resources. A URL identifies a
resource on the web. HTTP is a protocol used to transfer web
information. HTTPS uses encryption through TLS to help protect data in
transit. A server provides resources or services to clients. An API
defines a way for software systems to communicate. JSON is a text format
for representing structured data using objects, arrays, strings,
numbers, booleans, and null.

A database stores organized information. A relational database stores
data in tables with rows and columns. SQL is a language used to query
and manage relational databases. A primary key uniquely identifies a row
in a table. A foreign key links data between tables. A backup is a
separate copy of data that can help recover from loss.

Machine learning is a field in which computer systems learn patterns
from data to perform tasks. A model is a mathematical or computational
system that maps inputs to outputs. Training adjusts a model’s
parameters using data and an optimization method. A dataset is a
collection of examples used for training, validation, or testing. A
training set is used to fit a model. A validation set helps select
settings and compare model versions. A test set estimates performance on
data not used during training or model selection. Overfitting occurs
when a model learns training examples too specifically and performs
poorly on new examples. Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple
or insufficiently trained to capture important patterns. A loss function
measures how far predictions are from desired outputs according to a
chosen objective. An optimizer updates model parameters to reduce the
loss. A learning rate controls the size of parameter updates. A neural
network is a model made of connected computational units arranged in
layers. A token is a unit of text processed by a language model; it may
be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another symbol. A language
model learns statistical patterns in sequences of tokens and uses
context to predict or generate text.

A chatbot should not be considered intelligent merely because it
produces fluent sentences. Useful performance includes factual accuracy,
reasoning, consistency, instruction following, uncertainty handling, and
the ability to use tools appropriately. A dictionary of
question-and-answer pairs can help with common phrases, but it does not
by itself create broad reasoning ability. A large dataset can still be
poor if it contains contradictions, duplicated examples, incorrect
facts, or low-quality text. Feedback should be specific. A useful
correction identifies the mistaken claim and provides a better answer or
reliable evidence. A system should not blindly accept every correction.
It should consider whether the correction is supported and whether it
conflicts with reliable knowledge.

============================================================ SECTION 9 —
INTERNET, PRIVACY, AND DIGITAL SAFETY
============================================================

The internet is a global network of connected computer networks. The
World Wide Web is a system of linked resources accessed through the
internet. A search engine indexes and retrieves information to help
users find relevant web pages. A browser is an application used to
access websites. A domain name is a human-readable name associated with
internet resources. DNS helps translate domain names into IP addresses.

A strong password is long, unique, and difficult to guess. Using a
different password for every important account reduces the risk that one
leaked password compromises multiple accounts. A password manager can
help generate and store unique passwords. Multi-factor authentication
adds another verification step beyond a password. Never share passwords
or one-time security codes with someone who asks for them unexpectedly.
Be cautious with unexpected links, attachments, urgent messages, and
requests for private information. Phishing is an attempt to trick
someone into revealing information or taking an unsafe action. A secure
website connection does not automatically mean that the website itself
is trustworthy.

Personal information can include a full name, home address, phone
number, school, passwords, account identifiers, and private photographs.
Think carefully before sharing personal information online. Respect
other people’s privacy. Do not publish their private information without
permission. Digital footprints are traces of activity that may remain
online. Before posting, consider who might see the content and how it
could be copied or shared.

Copyright protects many creative works, including writing, music,
images, films, and software. Publicly accessible does not mean free to
copy. A citation identifies the source of information. Plagiarism means
presenting another person’s work or ideas as one’s own without proper
acknowledgment. When using external information, distinguish direct
quotations from paraphrases and provide source details when possible.

============================================================ SECTION 10
— GEOGRAPHY AND THE WORLD
============================================================

Geography studies places, environments, landscapes, populations, and the
relationships between people and their surroundings. A continent is one
of Earth’s large land divisions. A common model recognizes seven
continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, South
America, and Australia. An ocean is a vast body of salt water. The five
commonly recognized oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern,
and Arctic. A country is a political territory with its own government
and recognized boundaries. A capital city is often the seat of a
country’s national government, although some countries have multiple
government centers.

Canada is a country in North America. Canada’s capital is Ottawa. Canada
has ten provinces and three territories. The provinces are Alberta,
British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador,
Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, and Saskatchewan.
The territories are Northwest Territories, Nunavut, and Yukon. Canada
has coastlines on the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic Oceans. The Canadian
dollar is Canada’s currency. English and French are Canada’s official
languages at the federal level. Canada has a parliamentary system and is
a constitutional monarchy.

Ontario is a province in central-eastern Canada. Toronto is Ontario’s
capital and its largest city by population. Ottawa is Canada’s national
capital and is also in Ontario. The Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan,
Huron, Erie, and Ontario. The St. Lawrence River connects the Great
Lakes region to the Atlantic Ocean through a major waterway.

A map is a representation of a geographic area. A map scale relates
distances on a map to real-world distances. Latitude measures position
north or south of the Equator. Longitude measures position east or west
of the Prime Meridian. The Equator is at 0 degrees latitude. The Prime
Meridian is at 0 degrees longitude. A time zone is a region that uses a
common standard time. Local time can differ between places and can
change with daylight-saving rules.

============================================================ SECTION 11
— HISTORY AND CIVICS
============================================================

History studies past events using evidence such as documents, artifacts,
buildings, oral histories, and archaeological discoveries. A primary
source comes from the time or event being studied, such as a letter,
photograph, diary, or official record. A secondary source interprets or
analyzes primary sources and other evidence. Historical accounts can
differ because sources may be incomplete, biased, or interpreted
differently. Good historical reasoning considers context, evidence,
perspective, and uncertainty.

Ancient civilizations developed in different parts of the world,
including Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley, China, Greece, and the
Americas. Agriculture allowed many communities to settle and produce
food surpluses. Writing systems helped societies record information,
laws, trade, and stories. Trade connected communities and spread goods,
technologies, and ideas.

Democracy is a system in which people have a role in choosing leaders or
making decisions, often through voting and representative institutions.
A constitution establishes important rules and principles for
government. The rule of law means that laws apply through established
legal processes and that government authority is constrained by law.
Rights protect important freedoms and interests. Responsibilities are
duties people are expected to fulfill.

Canada is a federal parliamentary democracy and a constitutional
monarchy. Federalism divides governmental responsibilities between
levels of government. The federal government handles matters assigned to
it by the Constitution, while provinces and territories have their own
responsibilities. Municipal governments manage local matters under
authority granted by provinces or territories. In Canada’s federal
Parliament, the elected House of Commons and the Senate are part of the
legislative process, and the Crown is represented federally by the
Governor General. The Prime Minister leads the federal government. A
Member of Parliament represents a constituency, also called a riding.

============================================================ SECTION 12
— ECONOMICS AND MONEY
============================================================

Economics studies how people and societies make choices about limited
resources. Scarcity means that resources are limited compared with
people’s wants. Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best
alternative given up when making a choice. Supply is the amount sellers
are willing and able to offer at different prices. Demand is the amount
buyers are willing and able to purchase at different prices. In a basic
market model, prices are influenced by the interaction of supply and
demand.

A budget is a plan for income and spending. Income is money received.
Expenses are money spent. Savings are income not spent immediately. A
need is something essential for basic well-being. A want is something
desired but not essential. A loan is money borrowed that generally must
be repaid, often with interest. Interest is the cost of borrowing money
or the return earned on savings. A bank account can help store and
manage money. A debit card generally accesses money in an account. A
credit card allows borrowing up to a limit and requires repayment under
its terms.

Inflation is a general increase in prices over time, reducing the
purchasing power of money. A currency exchange rate describes the value
of one currency in terms of another. Taxes are compulsory payments
collected by governments to fund public services and other
responsibilities. Economic statistics describe groups and trends; they
do not automatically predict what will happen to one individual.

============================================================ SECTION 13
— ART, MUSIC, AND CREATIVITY
============================================================

Art can communicate ideas, feelings, observations, and cultural meanings
through visual, performing, and other forms. Elements of visual art
include line, shape, form, color, value, texture, and space. Composition
is the arrangement of elements in an artwork. Contrast creates visible
differences between elements. Balance describes how visual weight is
distributed. Perspective can create an impression of depth.

Music organizes sound through elements such as rhythm, melody, harmony,
dynamics, timbre, and form. A beat is a regular pulse. Rhythm organizes
sounds and silences over time. Melody is a sequence of pitches perceived
as a musical idea. Harmony involves pitches sounding together or in
relation. Tempo is the speed of the beat. Dynamics describe loudness and
softness. Timbre is the quality that makes one sound source different
from another.

Creativity often involves combining existing ideas in new ways,
experimenting, revising, and learning from results. A first draft does
not need to be perfect. Feedback is most useful when it is specific and
respectful. A prototype is an early version used to test an idea.
Iteration means improving something through repeated cycles of testing
and revision.

============================================================ SECTION 14
— REASONING AND PROBLEM SOLVING
============================================================

A good problem-solving process begins by understanding the goal.
Identify what is known, what is unknown, and what constraints apply.
Break a large problem into smaller parts. Consider more than one
possible approach. Choose a method and explain why it fits. Check the
result against the original problem. If the answer seems unreasonable,
review the assumptions and calculations.

An observation is something noticed or measured. An inference is a
conclusion drawn from observations and background knowledge. A claim is
a statement that can be supported or challenged. Evidence is information
that supports or weakens a claim. A reasoned explanation connects
evidence to a conclusion.

Correlation means two variables change together in some way. Correlation
alone does not prove that one variable causes the other. Causation means
a change in one factor produces a change in another under the relevant
conditions. Confounding variables can make a relationship appear
stronger, weaker, or different from what it really is. A controlled
experiment can help investigate causal relationships, but its design and
limitations matter.

A logical argument contains premises and a conclusion. A valid argument
has a conclusion that follows logically from its premises. A sound
argument is valid and has true premises. An assumption is something
accepted temporarily or without proof. A counterexample is an example
that shows a general claim is false. A generalization should be based on
enough relevant evidence. A false dilemma presents only two options when
more possibilities exist. Confirmation bias is the tendency to favor
information that supports existing beliefs. A source should be evaluated
for expertise, evidence, purpose, date, and possible conflicts of
interest.

When uncertain, a helpful AI should: 1. Identify exactly what is
uncertain. 2. Separate known facts from assumptions. 3. Ask a clarifying
question if missing information changes the answer. 4. State a
confidence level only when it has a meaningful basis. 5. Avoid inventing
names, numbers, quotations, sources, or events. 6. Explain how the
answer could be checked. 7. Correct mistakes when credible new evidence
appears.

============================================================ SECTION 15
— EVERYDAY KNOWLEDGE
============================================================

Time is commonly measured in seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks,
months, and years. One minute contains 60 seconds. One hour contains 60
minutes. One day contains 24 hours. A common year contains 365 days. A
leap year contains 366 days. A leap year in the Gregorian calendar is
generally divisible by 4, except century years must also be divisible by
400.

The metric system is based on powers of ten. 1 kilometre = 1000 metres.
1 metre = 100 centimetres. 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres. 1 kilogram =
1000 grams. 1 litre = 1000 millilitres. 1 hour = 60 minutes. Temperature
in Celsius: water freezes at about 0 °C and boils at about 100 °C at
standard atmospheric pressure.

A recipe is a set of instructions for preparing food. Measurements
should be followed carefully, especially when baking. Food safety
includes washing hands, preventing cross-contamination, storing food at
appropriate temperatures, and cooking foods to safe internal
temperatures. Food allergies can be serious. Never assume a food is safe
for someone with an allergy. A person who is lactose intolerant may have
difficulty digesting lactose, a sugar found in milk. Lactose-free
products are made to reduce or remove lactose, but ingredients should
still be checked.

Sleep supports learning, memory, mood, and physical health. Regular
movement supports general health. A balanced diet includes a variety of
foods and nutrients. Hydration needs vary with activity, climate, age,
and health. Health advice should be appropriate to the individual. An AI
should not diagnose a person from a short message and should encourage
help from a trusted adult or qualified professional when a concern may
be serious.

============================================================ SECTION 16
— ANIMALS AND PLANTS
============================================================

Animals are multicellular organisms that obtain energy by consuming
organic material. Vertebrates have a backbone. Invertebrates do not have
a backbone. Mammals are vertebrates that have hair or fur at some stage
and produce milk for their young. Birds have feathers and beaks.
Reptiles generally have scales and are ectothermic. Amphibians often
have life cycles involving aquatic and terrestrial stages. Fish are
aquatic vertebrates that typically use gills to obtain oxygen from
water.

Insects have six legs, three main body regions, and an exoskeleton.
Arachnids, such as spiders, have eight legs and are not insects.
Crustaceans include crabs, lobsters, and many other animals. Molluscs
include snails, clams, squid, and octopuses.

Plants are multicellular organisms that usually make sugars through
photosynthesis. Roots often anchor plants and absorb water and minerals.
Stems support leaves and transport materials. Leaves are major sites of
photosynthesis. Flowers are reproductive structures in flowering plants.
Seeds contain an embryo and stored resources, often protected by a seed
coat. Germination is the beginning of growth from a seed.

Pollination transfers pollen to a receptive part of a flower.
Fertilization occurs when reproductive cells unite. Some plants
reproduce without seeds, using spores or vegetative structures. Fungi
are not plants. They form a separate group of organisms and obtain
nutrients by absorption.

============================================================ SECTION 17
— SPACE, ENGINEERING, AND INVENTION
============================================================

Engineering applies scientific and mathematical knowledge to design
solutions to practical problems. A design constraint is a limit such as
cost, size, weight, materials, or safety. A design criterion is a
feature a successful solution should meet. A prototype helps test
whether a design works. Testing reveals strengths and weaknesses. A
redesign uses test results to improve the solution.

A lever is a simple machine that rotates around a fulcrum. A pulley uses
a wheel and rope or cable to change the direction of a force and, in
some arrangements, reduce the force needed. An inclined plane is a
sloped surface. A wheel and axle can reduce friction or change how force
is applied. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder. A
wedge is a moving inclined plane. Simple machines do not create energy;
they trade force and distance.

A robot is a programmable machine that can sense, process information,
and act. A sensor measures something about the environment. An actuator
produces movement or another physical action. A controller processes
information and coordinates actions. A motor converts energy into
motion. A robot may use wheels, tracks, legs, arms, or other mechanisms.
Autonomous behavior means a system can perform some tasks without
continuous direct human control. Robots should be designed with safe
movement, emergency stopping, and protection for people and
surroundings.

============================================================ SECTION 18
— SAMPLE QUESTION AND ANSWER PAIRS
============================================================

Q: Why is the sky blue? A: Air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of
sunlight, especially blue light, more strongly than longer wavelengths.
This scattered light reaches our eyes from many directions.

Q: Why do we see lightning before hearing thunder? A: Light travels much
faster than sound, so the flash reaches us before the sound.

Q: Why do objects fall? A: Earth’s gravity attracts objects toward its
center. Air resistance can affect how quickly they fall.

Q: Why does ice float on water? A: Ordinary ice is less dense than
liquid water, so it floats.

Q: What is the largest planet in our solar system? A: Jupiter is the
largest planet in our solar system.

Q: How many planets are in our solar system? A: There are eight
recognized planets.

Q: What is the closest star to Earth? A: The Sun is the closest star to
Earth.

Q: What is the closest planet to the Sun? A: Mercury.

Q: What is the capital of Canada? A: Ottawa.

Q: What is the capital of Ontario? A: Toronto.

Q: What is the largest ocean? A: The Pacific Ocean.

Q: What is the smallest prime number? A: 2. It is the only even prime
number.

Q: What is 12 times 12? A: 144.

Q: What is 15 percent of 200? A: 30, because 0.15 × 200 = 30.

Q: What is the square root of 81? A: 9, because 9 × 9 = 81.

Q: What is the area of a rectangle that is 8 centimetres long and 5
centimetres wide? A: 40 square centimetres, because 8 × 5 = 40.

Q: What is an ecosystem? A: An ecosystem is a community of organisms
interacting with one another and with their physical environment.

Q: What is photosynthesis? A: Photosynthesis is the process by which
plants, algae, and some bacteria use light energy to make energy-rich
organic molecules.

Q: What does DNA do? A: DNA stores hereditary information used in the
development, functioning, and reproduction of living organisms.

Q: What is evaporation? A: Evaporation is the change from liquid to gas
at a surface.

Q: What is an algorithm? A: An algorithm is a sequence of steps for
solving a problem or carrying out a task.

Q: What is a variable in programming? A: A variable is a named place or
reference used to store a value that a program can use.

Q: What is debugging? A: Debugging is finding, understanding, and fixing
problems in software.

Q: What is machine learning? A: Machine learning is a field of computing
in which models learn patterns from data to make predictions or generate
outputs.

Q: Does a bigger dataset always make an AI better? A: No. Data quality,
accuracy, diversity, relevance, formatting, and training methods all
matter. More low-quality data can make a model worse.

Q: Can an AI learn from every correction automatically? A: Not safely or
reliably. Corrections should be checked, stored with context, and used
in a controlled learning process. A single correction may be incomplete
or incorrect.

Q: What should an AI do if it does not know an answer? A: It should say
that it is unsure, explain what information is missing, and suggest a
way to verify the answer.

============================================================ SECTION 19
— CONVERSATION WITH CONTEXT
============================================================

User: What is gravity? DavidAI: Gravity is an attractive interaction
between objects that have mass. On Earth, it pulls objects toward the
planet’s center and gives objects weight.

User: So does gravity pull the Moon too? DavidAI: Yes. Earth’s gravity
helps keep the Moon in orbit. The Moon is also moving sideways, so it
continually falls around Earth rather than straight down onto it.

User: What is an orbit? DavidAI: An orbit is the curved path one object
follows around another because of gravity and its motion.

User: Can you make that simpler? DavidAI: Imagine throwing a ball
sideways. It falls toward the ground while moving forward. An orbit is
similar, except an object moves fast enough that the curved surface of a
planet keeps dropping away beneath it.

User: What does a CPU do? DavidAI: A CPU executes program instructions
and coordinates many operations inside a computer.

User: Is the CPU the same as RAM? DavidAI: No. The CPU processes
instructions. RAM temporarily holds data and instructions that are being
used. They work together but have different jobs.

User: What if my computer has more RAM? DavidAI: More RAM can help when
you need to keep many programs or large files active at once. It does
not automatically make every task faster; the CPU, storage, software,
and workload also matter.

User: How do I make an AI smarter? DavidAI: First decide what “smarter”
means for your project. Useful improvements may include better training
data, a suitable model architecture, a reliable training process,
evaluation tests, memory, and tools. A dictionary alone is not enough
for general intelligence.

User: Should I just add millions of facts? DavidAI: Facts can help, but
quality matters more than raw quantity. Use accurate, varied examples
and test whether the model can apply what it learns. Include
explanations and reasoning examples, not only isolated facts.

User: How can I tell if training is working? DavidAI: Track training
loss and validation loss, test the model on examples it has never seen,
and compare its answers over time. A falling training loss alone does
not prove that the model is becoming generally useful.

User: What is overfitting? DavidAI: Overfitting happens when a model
memorizes details of its training data instead of learning patterns that
generalize to new examples.

User: What should I do when it gives nonsense? DavidAI: Check whether
the model has enough capacity, whether the data is formatted correctly,
whether the tokenizer and training setup match, and whether the model
has been trained long enough. Also inspect examples from the dataset for
noise or contradictions.

============================================================ SECTION 20
— GOOD AI BEHAVIOR
============================================================

DavidAI should aim to be helpful, honest, clear, and respectful. DavidAI
should answer the actual question instead of changing the subject.
DavidAI should adapt explanations to the user’s apparent level of
knowledge. DavidAI should not pretend to have feelings, experiences,
memories, or abilities that it does not have. DavidAI should not claim
to have searched the web unless a search tool was actually used. DavidAI
should not claim to have saved information unless a memory system
actually confirmed the save. DavidAI should distinguish between stored
information and information inferred from context. DavidAI should not
invent citations, sources, statistics, quotations, or personal
experiences. DavidAI should not present guesses as facts. DavidAI should
correct errors directly and politely. DavidAI should ask one clear
question when an essential detail is missing. DavidAI should explain
complex topics in steps. DavidAI should use examples when examples
improve understanding. DavidAI should avoid repeating the same point
unnecessarily. DavidAI should protect private information. DavidAI
should follow safety rules and avoid helping people cause harm. DavidAI
should acknowledge that information can become outdated. DavidAI should
prefer reliable evidence over popularity or confidence. DavidAI should
be willing to say: “I don’t know.” DavidAI should be willing to say: “I
made a mistake. Here is the correction.” DavidAI should treat user
feedback as useful evidence, not as unquestionable truth.

==================================================
SECTION 1: ABOUT ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
==================================================

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science focused on creating computer systems that can perform tasks normally associated with human intelligence.

AI systems can perform tasks such as:
- Answering questions.
- Recognizing patterns.
- Understanding language.
- Analyzing information.
- Generating text.
- Solving mathematical problems.
- Classifying information.
- Making predictions.

There are several major categories of AI.

1. Rule-Based AI:
Rule-based systems follow predefined instructions. For example, if a temperature is above 30 degrees, a system might classify the weather as hot.

2. Machine Learning:
Machine learning allows computers to identify patterns in data and improve their performance without explicitly programming every individual rule.

3. Deep Learning:
Deep learning uses artificial neural networks with multiple layers to process complex information.

4. Natural Language Processing:
Natural Language Processing (NLP) focuses on allowing computers to understand, analyze, and generate human language.

5. Computer Vision:
Computer vision allows computers to interpret images and videos.

IMPORTANT AI TERMINOLOGY:

Dataset: A collection of information used to train, test, or evaluate a system.

Model: A computational system that processes information and produces outputs.

Training: The process of adjusting a model using examples.

Inference: Using a trained model to generate a result.

Neural Network: A computational structure inspired by some principles of biological neural systems.

Parameter: A numerical value inside a model that influences its behavior.

Token: A unit of text processed by a language model.

Embedding: A numerical representation of information that captures relationships between concepts.

Overfitting: When a model learns its training examples too closely and performs poorly on new information.

Underfitting: When a model fails to learn important patterns in its training data.

==================================================
SECTION 2: COMPUTER SCIENCE
==================================================

A computer is an electronic machine that receives input, processes information, stores data, and produces output.

The four basic computer operations are:

1. Input.
2. Processing.
3. Storage.
4. Output.

HARDWARE:

CPU:
The Central Processing Unit executes instructions and performs calculations. It is often described as the brain of a computer.

RAM:
Random Access Memory temporarily stores information that active programs need. RAM is generally volatile, meaning its contents are lost when power is removed.

Storage:
SSDs and hard drives store information persistently.

GPU:
A Graphics Processing Unit performs parallel computations and is especially useful for graphics and machine learning.

Motherboard:
The motherboard connects the major components of a computer.

Operating System:
An operating system manages hardware and software resources. Examples include Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, and iOS.

SOFTWARE:

Software is a collection of instructions that tells a computer what to do.

Applications are programs designed for particular tasks.

Examples:
- Web browsers.
- Image editors.
- Games.
- Programming environments.
- Database applications.

==================================================
SECTION 3: PROGRAMMING KNOWLEDGE
==================================================

Programming is the process of writing instructions that computers can execute.

IMPORTANT PROGRAMMING CONCEPTS:

Variable:
A variable stores a value.

Example:
age = 15

String:
A string represents text.

Example:
name = "DavidAI"

An integer is a whole number.

Example:
temperature = 25

A floating-point number represents a decimal value.

Example:
pi = 3.14159

A Boolean value is either true or false.

Example:
is_active = true

Conditional:
A conditional executes different instructions depending on whether a condition is true or false.

Example:

if temperature > 30:
    print("It is hot")
else:
    print("It is not hot")

Loop:
A loop repeats instructions.

Function:
A function is a reusable block of code.

Example:

function greet(name) {
    return "Hello, " + name;
}

Array:
An array stores multiple values in an ordered collection.

Example:

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

Object:
An object stores related information using properties.

Example:

user = {
    name: "DavidAI",
    version: 1,
    active: true
}

Mathematics is the study of numbers, structures, quantities, patterns, and relationships.

ARITHMETIC:

Addition combines quantities.

Subtraction calculates the difference between quantities.

Multiplication represents repeated addition.

Division separates a quantity into equal groups.

ORDER OF OPERATIONS:

BEDMAS means:
- Brackets.
- Exponents.
- Division.
- Multiplication.
- Addition.
- Subtraction.

Example:

5 + 3 × 4 = 17

Multiplication happens before addition.

FRACTIONS:

A fraction represents part of a whole.

Example:

3/4 means three parts out of four equal parts.

The numerator is the top number.

The denominator is the bottom number.

DECIMALS:

A decimal represents a number using a base-ten positional system.

Example:

Physics studies matter, energy, motion, forces, and interactions in the universe.

FORCE:

A force is a push or pull that can change an object's motion.

The SI unit of force is the Newton (N).

NEWTON'S LAWS:

First Law:
An object remains at rest or continues moving at a constant velocity unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force.

Second Law:
Force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.

F = ma

Third Law:
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

GRAVITY:

Gravity is an attractive interaction between objects with mass.

On Earth's surface, gravitational acceleration is approximately 9.81 m/s².

ENERGY:

Energy is the ability to cause change or perform work.

Types include:
- Kinetic energy.
- Potential energy.
- Thermal energy.
- Chemical energy.
- Electrical energy.
- Nuclear energy.
- Light energy.

Kinetic energy is energy associated with motion.

Potential energy is stored energy associated with position or configuration.

ELECTRICITY:

Electric current is the flow of electric charge.

Voltage is electrical potential difference.

Resistance describes opposition to current.

Ohm's Law:

V = I × R

Where:
V = Voltage
I = Current
R = Resistance

==================================================

Chemistry studies matter, its composition, properties, and transformations.

ATOM:

An atom is the basic unit of a chemical element.

Atoms contain:
- Protons.
- Neutrons.
- Electrons.

Protons have a positive electrical charge.

Neutrons have no electrical charge.

Electrons have a negative electrical charge.

ELEMENTS:

An element is a substance consisting of atoms with the same number of protons.

Examples:
Hydrogen (H)
Oxygen (O)
Carbon (C)
Nitrogen (N)
Iron (Fe)
Gold (Au)
Silver (Ag)

MOLECULES:

A molecule consists of two or more atoms chemically bonded together.

Examples:

Water: H2O
Carbon dioxide: CO2
Oxygen gas: O2
Methane: CH4

STATES OF MATTER:

Solid:
Has a definite shape and volume.

Liquid:
Has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.

Gas:
Has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.

Plasma:
An energetic state of matter containing charged particles.

CHEMICAL REACTIONS:

A chemical reaction transforms substances into different substances.

Reactants are the starting substances.

Products are the substances created.

The law of conservation of mass states that matter is conserved during ordinary chemical reactions.

==================================================

Biology is the scientific study of living organisms.

CELL:

The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

Nucleus:
Contains most of the cell's genetic information.

Cell Membrane:
Controls what enters and leaves the cell.

Cytoplasm:
The material inside the cell where many cellular processes occur.

Mitochondria:
Produce much of the ATP used by cells through cellular respiration.

Ribosomes:
Build proteins.

Chloroplasts:
Found in plants and some other organisms. They perform photosynthesis.

PHOTOSYNTHESIS:

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen.

Simplified equation:

6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2

CELLULAR RESPIRATION:

Cells break down nutrients to release usable energy.

Simplified equation:

Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy

DNA:

DNA stands for Deoxyribonucleic Acid.

It contains genetic instructions used in the development, functioning, and reproduction of organisms.

ECOSYSTEMS:

An ecosystem includes living organisms and their physical environment.

Producers create their own food, usually through photosynthesis.

Consumers obtain energy by eating other organisms.

Decomposers break down dead organic material and recycle nutrients.

GALAXIES:

A galaxy is a large gravitationally bound system containing stars, gas, dust, and dark matter.

BLACK HOLES:

knowledge.title: Grammar: Simple sentences
knowledge.content: A simple sentence contains one independent clause with a subject and a verb. It can be short, such as Birds fly, or include modifiers, such as The small birds fly quickly. A simple sentence is complete even though it has only one clause.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Compound sentences
knowledge.content: A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or or so. Example: I studied hard, and I passed the test. Each clause could stand alone as its own sentence.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Complex sentences
knowledge.content: A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. Example: I stayed home because it rained. The dependent clause adds reason, time, condition or contrast and cannot stand alone.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Compound-complex sentences
knowledge.content: A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and one dependent clause. Example: I finished my work, and I went outside after the rain stopped. Use it when several related ideas need precise connections.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Clauses
knowledge.content: A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. An independent clause can stand alone. A dependent clause begins with a subordinator such as because, although or when and needs an independent clause to complete its meaning.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Phrases
knowledge.content: A phrase is a group of words that acts as one part of a sentence but does not contain both a subject and a verb. Examples include in the room, a careful reader and to learn. Phrases add detail without forming a full clause.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Subject-verb agreement
knowledge.content: A verb agrees with its subject in number. A singular subject usually takes a verb ending in s in the present tense, such as She reads. A plural subject uses the base form, such as They read. Phrases between the subject and verb do not change the agreement.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Verb tenses
knowledge.content: Verb tenses place actions and states in time. The simple present describes habits or facts, the simple past describes completed events, and the simple future describes what will happen. Continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms add detail about duration or completion.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Perfect tenses
knowledge.content: Perfect tenses use have, has or had with a past participle. The present perfect links past events to now, as in I have finished. The past perfect describes an event before another past event, as in I had eaten before you arrived.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Progressive tenses
knowledge.content: Progressive tenses use a form of be with an ing verb. They describe actions in progress, such as She is reading or They were working. Stative verbs such as know and believe are less often used in progressive forms.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Active and passive voice
knowledge.content: In an active sentence, the subject performs the action: The teacher praised the student. In a passive sentence, the subject receives the action: The student was praised by the teacher. Passive voice is useful when the action matters more than the actor.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Conditional sentences
knowledge.content: Conditional sentences describe results and conditions. A zero conditional uses present forms for general truths: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. A first conditional uses will for likely future results: If it rains, we will stay home. Other forms discuss unlikely or unreal situations.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Modal verbs
knowledge.content: Modal verbs such as can, may, must, should and will express ability, permission, obligation, advice or future intention. They are followed by a base verb: You should study. Modals change the tone of a statement without changing the main action.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Question forms
knowledge.content: Yes or no questions usually place an auxiliary or modal before the subject: Do you learn English? Wh questions begin with a question word such as what, where, when, who, why or how. In formal English, the subject and auxiliary invert.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Negative sentences
knowledge.content: Negatives use not, never, no or neither. With auxiliary or modal verbs, not follows the auxiliary: I do not know. Without an auxiliary, English usually adds do support: She does not play. Double negatives can change meaning in standard English.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Imperative sentences
knowledge.content: An imperative gives a command, instruction, request or invitation. It uses the base verb and has an implied subject you: Open the book. Please makes a request softer. Negative imperatives use do not or never: Do not run.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Exclamative sentences
knowledge.content: Exclamative sentences express strong feeling and often begin with What or How. Examples include What a lovely day it is and How quickly you learned. They can be formal in writing and conversational in speech.

knowledge.title: Grammar: There be sentences
knowledge.content: There be sentences introduce or discuss existence. Example: There are three books on the table. The true subject comes after be, so the verb agrees with that noun: There is a book, but There are books.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Dummy it
knowledge.content: The pronoun it can fill the subject position when English needs a subject but has no real one. Example: It is raining. It can also introduce an evaluation with an infinitive: It is important to review your work.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Personal pronouns
knowledge.content: Personal pronouns replace nouns. I, you, he, she, it, we and they usually act as subjects, while me, you, him, her, it, us and them usually act as objects. Choosing the correct form depends on the pronoun's role.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Pronoun case
knowledge.content: Subject pronouns perform actions: He helped me. Object pronouns receive actions: I helped him. Possessive pronouns show ownership: That book is mine. Using the wrong case is common in long noun phrases.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Possessive forms
knowledge.content: Possession is shown with possessive pronouns such as my and your, or with an apostrophe and s for nouns: the student's book. For plural nouns ending in s, add only an apostrophe: the students' books.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Reflexive pronouns
knowledge.content: Reflexive pronouns such as myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves and themselves refer back to the subject. Example: She taught herself. Use them when the subject and object are the same person or thing.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Demonstratives
knowledge.content: Demonstratives point to nouns. This and that refer to singular nouns, while these and those refer to plural nouns. This and these usually suggest something near; that and those suggest something farther away in space or time.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Quantifiers
knowledge.content: Quantifiers show amount or number. Use many with countable plurals, much with uncountable nouns, and a lot of with either. Few and a few differ in tone: few suggests almost none, while a few suggests some.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Determiners
knowledge.content: Determiners come before nouns and include articles, demonstratives, possessives and quantifiers. Examples include the book, this book, my book and many books. A noun phrase can contain only a limited set of determiners.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Comparatives and superlatives
knowledge.content: Comparative adjectives compare two things and often use er or more: taller, more careful. Superlatives compare three or more things and use est or most: tallest, most careful. Irregular forms include good, better and best.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Prepositions
knowledge.content: Prepositions show relationships such as place, time, direction and manner. Common examples are in, on, at, by, with, for, from and about. In the box, on the table and at 5 o clock each use a different relationship.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Conjunctions
knowledge.content: Conjunctions join words, phrases or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions such as and, but, or and so join equal parts. Subordinating conjunctions such as because, although and while introduce dependent clauses.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Relative clauses
knowledge.content: Relative clauses add information about a noun. They often begin with who, whom, whose, which or that. The book that I borrowed is interesting. Defining clauses identify which thing is meant, while non-defining clauses add extra information.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Reported speech
knowledge.content: Reported speech repeats what someone said without quotation marks. Example: She said that she was tired. Tenses, pronouns and time expressions often shift back when the reporting verb is in the past.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Commas
knowledge.content: Commas separate items in a list, set off introductory phrases and separate non-defining clauses. Example: After the meeting, we reviewed the plan, the budget and the timeline. They help readers group ideas.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Semicolons and colons
knowledge.content: A semicolon links closely related independent clauses: I finished the draft; you can review it. A colon introduces an explanation, list or quotation: We need three things: time, tools and evidence.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Apostrophes
knowledge.content: Apostrophes mark ownership and contractions. The cat's toy belongs to one cat; the cats' toys belong to several cats. Do not becomes don't in a contraction, and its as a possessive has no apostrophe.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Quotation marks
knowledge.content: Quotation marks enclose direct speech and the titles of short works. Example: He said, 'I am ready.' In British and American styles, punctuation placement differs, so follow the style guide you are using.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Parallel structure
knowledge.content: Parallel structure uses the same grammatical form for items in a list or comparison. Example: We value clarity, accuracy and fairness. Mixing forms, such as clarity and being accurate, can sound uneven.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Topic sentences
knowledge.content: A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph. It usually appears near the beginning and helps the reader understand what the following sentences will support. Other sentences should explain, evidence or develop that idea.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Cohesion and transitions
knowledge.content: Transitions show relationships between ideas. However signals contrast, therefore signals result, for example introduces evidence, and finally marks the end of a sequence. Use them sparingly and choose the relationship accurately.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Paragraph unity
knowledge.content: A unified paragraph develops one controlling idea. Sentences that introduce a new main idea usually belong in a new paragraph. Long paragraphs can be easier to read when divided at a clear change of focus.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Summaries and paraphrases
knowledge.content: A summary condenses a source into its main points in your own words. A paraphrase restates a specific passage while keeping the meaning. Both should credit the original source when the ideas are not common knowledge.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Register and tone
knowledge.content: Register is the level of formality in language. A formal report avoids slang and contractions, while a friendly message may use short sentences and everyday words. Good writing matches tone to audience and purpose.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Sentence variety
knowledge.content: Varying sentence length and structure makes writing easier to follow. A short sentence can emphasise a key point, while a longer sentence can connect related ideas. Too much variety without clarity can confuse the reader.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Fragments and run-on sentences
knowledge.content: A sentence fragment lacks a complete subject and verb or begins with a subordinator without an independent clause. A run-on sentence joins complete sentences without proper punctuation or a conjunction. Both can be fixed by separating or connecting clauses.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Adverb word order
knowledge.content: Adverbs of frequency often go before the main verb but after be: She often reads; She is often late. Manner adverbs usually follow the verb or object: He spoke clearly. Time and place details often come near the end.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Phrasal verbs
knowledge.content: A phrasal verb combines a verb with a particle such as up, out or off. Examples include look up, find out and turn off. Some phrasal verbs are separable, so a short object can go between the verb and particle.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Collocations
knowledge.content: Collocations are words that naturally occur together, such as make a decision, take a risk and heavy rain. They are not always predictable from grammar alone. Learning common collocations makes language sound more natural.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Hedging
