knowledge.content: Hedging uses careful language such as may, might, seems, suggests and in some cases. It shows appropriate uncertainty when evidence is limited. Clear writing still states what is known before describing what is uncertain.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Defining terms
knowledge.content: A good definition names the category a thing belongs to and the features that distinguish it from others. Example: A triangle is a polygon with three sides and three angles. Avoid using the word being defined inside its own definition.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Explaining processes
knowledge.content: Process explanations list steps in a clear order. Signal words such as first, next, then and finally help readers follow the sequence. Each step should state both the action and its result.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Comparing and contrasting
knowledge.content: Comparison shows similarities; contrast shows differences. Useful language includes similarly, in the same way, however, whereas and on the other hand. Make clear what is being compared and on which point.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Cellular respiration
knowledge.content: Cellular respiration is the process cells use to release energy from food. In many organisms, oxygen helps convert glucose into carbon dioxide and water, producing ATP that powers cell activities. It happens in mitochondria and is different from photosynthesis, which stores energy.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Mitosis and meiosis
knowledge.content: Mitosis produces two genetically identical body cells for growth and repair. Meiosis produces sex cells with half the usual number of chromosomes, increasing genetic variation. Mistakes in these processes can lead to cells with abnormal chromosome numbers.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Inheritance patterns
knowledge.content: Dominant alleles can mask recessive alleles when both are present. Recessive traits usually appear only when an individual has two copies of the recessive allele. Punnett squares predict probabilities of inherited traits, not guaranteed outcomes for each child.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Evolution and natural selection
knowledge.content: Evolution is change in the inherited traits of populations over generations. Natural selection occurs when individuals with helpful heritable traits tend to survive and reproduce more successfully. Evolution acts on populations, not on individual organisms during their lifetimes.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Biodiversity
knowledge.content: Biodiversity is the variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem levels. It supports services such as pollination, nutrient cycling, clean water and resilience to change. Habitat loss, pollution, overuse and climate change can reduce biodiversity.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Microorganisms
knowledge.content: Microorganisms include bacteria, archaea, many fungi, algae and protozoa. They are too small to see clearly without a microscope. Many are harmless or beneficial, helping decompose matter, make food and support ecosystems.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Viruses and bacteria
knowledge.content: Bacteria are single-celled living organisms that can reproduce on their own. Viruses are much smaller and need host cells to reproduce. Antibiotics can treat many bacterial infections but do not work against viruses.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Vaccines and immunity
knowledge.content: Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the full disease. They can reduce the risk of severe illness and help protect people who cannot be vaccinated. Immunity varies by vaccine, person and time.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Antibiotic resistance
knowledge.content: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria change so medicines that once worked become less effective. Unnecessary or incomplete use of antibiotics can encourage resistant strains. Taking antibiotics only when prescribed helps slow resistance.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Plant structures
knowledge.content: Roots anchor plants and absorb water and minerals. Stems support leaves and transport materials, while leaves carry out much of photosynthesis. Flowers, fruits and seeds help plants reproduce and disperse.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Animal adaptations
knowledge.content: Adaptations are features that help organisms survive and reproduce in their environments. Camouflage, migrations, specialised beaks and nocturnal habits are examples. Adaptations arise over many generations through inherited variation and selection.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Human senses
knowledge.content: The senses gather information about the environment. Eyes detect light, ears detect sound waves, the nose and tongue detect chemicals, and skin detects pressure, temperature and pain. The brain interprets these signals to guide behaviour.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Chemical bonds
knowledge.content: Chemical bonds hold atoms together in molecules and crystals. Ionic bonds involve the transfer of electrons, covalent bonds involve sharing electrons, and metallic bonds involve delocalised electrons. Bond type helps determine properties such as melting point and conductivity.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Acids and bases
knowledge.content: Acids release hydrogen ions in water and have a pH below 7. Bases accept hydrogen ions or release hydroxide ions and have a pH above 7. A pH of 7 is neutral, and strong acids or bases require careful handling.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Solutions and mixtures
knowledge.content: A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which a solute is dissolved in a solvent. Other mixtures, such as sand in water, are heterogeneous and can often be separated by filtering. Solubility can change with temperature.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Temperature scales
knowledge.content: Celsius sets water's freezing point at 0 degrees and boiling point at 100 degrees at standard pressure. Fahrenheit uses 32 and 212 degrees for those points. Kelvin starts at absolute zero and is commonly used in science.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Electric circuits
knowledge.content: An electric circuit needs a closed path for current to flow. Voltage provides the push, current is the flow of charge, and resistance limits the flow. Series circuits share one path; parallel circuits provide multiple paths.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Magnetism
knowledge.content: Magnets create magnetic fields and attract certain materials such as iron. Every magnet has a north and south pole; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Electric currents can produce magnetic fields, which is how electromagnets work.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Waves
knowledge.content: A wave transfers energy without permanently moving the medium as a whole. In transverse waves, oscillations are perpendicular to travel direction; in longitudinal waves, they are parallel. Amplitude relates to energy and wavelength relates to frequency.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Electromagnetic spectrum
knowledge.content: The electromagnetic spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X rays and gamma rays. All travel through space at the speed of light. Higher frequency waves generally carry more energy and can be more penetrating.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Nuclear energy
knowledge.content: Nuclear energy is released in reactions involving atomic nuclei. Fission splits heavy nuclei, while fusion combines light nuclei. Nuclear power produces large amounts of energy but requires careful management of radioactive materials.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Plate tectonics
knowledge.content: Earth's outer shell is divided into plates that move slowly over the mantle. Plates can diverge, converge or slide past one another. Their movement shapes mountains, earthquakes, volcanoes and ocean basins.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Earthquakes and volcanoes
knowledge.content: Earthquakes happen when stress on rocks causes sudden rupture and release of energy. Volcanoes form when magma reaches the surface. Both are common near plate boundaries, though some occur within plates.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Rock cycle
knowledge.content: The rock cycle describes how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks change over time. Melting, cooling, weathering, erosion, compaction and heat drive the transformations. Rocks can follow different paths depending on conditions.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Telescopes
knowledge.content: Telescopes collect and focus light or other radiation from distant objects. Optical telescopes use lenses or mirrors, while radio telescopes detect radio waves. Larger collectors can detect fainter objects and reveal more detail.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Exoplanets
knowledge.content: Exoplanets are planets outside our solar system. Astronomers detect them by observing small dips in starlight, gravitational wobble or other subtle effects. Many known exoplanets differ greatly from the planets in our solar system.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Black holes
knowledge.content: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that light cannot escape past its event horizon. Black holes can form when massive stars collapse. They can be detected by their effects on nearby stars and glowing material.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Big bang model
knowledge.content: The big bang model describes the expansion of the universe from a very hot, dense early state. Evidence includes the expansion of galaxies, the cosmic microwave background and the abundance of light elements. It does not describe everything before that early state.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Space probes
knowledge.content: Space probes are robotic spacecraft sent to study planets, moons, comets and other bodies. They can carry cameras, spectrometers and other instruments. Probes often provide closer and longer observations than telescopes from Earth.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Satellites and orbits
knowledge.content: Satellites orbit planets because their forward motion balances gravitational pull. Artificial satellites support communication, navigation, weather observation and research. Orbit height affects speed, coverage and how long a satellite remains useful.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Comets and asteroids
knowledge.content: Asteroids are rocky objects mostly found between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy objects that can develop tails when they approach the Sun. Both are remnants from the early solar system.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Stellar life cycle
knowledge.content: Stars form from clouds of gas and dust. A star like the Sun spends most of its life fusing hydrogen into helium, then expands into a red giant and later becomes a white dwarf. More massive stars can end in supernovae.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Vectors
knowledge.content: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Vectors can represent forces, velocities and displacements. Adding vectors requires combining components, and a vector can be scaled by multiplying each component.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Matrices
knowledge.content: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. Matrices can represent transformations and systems of linear equations. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so order matters.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Logarithms
knowledge.content: A logarithm answers the question of what exponent produces a given number. If 2 to the power of 3 equals 8, then log base 2 of 8 equals 3. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition and are useful for very large ranges.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Exponential growth and decay
knowledge.content: Exponential growth occurs when a quantity increases by a fixed percentage or factor in each time period. Doubling is a common example. Exponential decay describes a quantity decreasing by a fixed factor, such as radioactive half life.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Polynomials
knowledge.content: A polynomial is an expression made of terms with whole number powers of a variable. The highest power is its degree. Polynomials can be added, subtracted, multiplied, divided and factored.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Rational functions
knowledge.content: A rational function is a ratio of two polynomials. Its graph can have vertical asymptotes where the denominator is zero and horizontal or slant asymptotes that describe end behaviour. Values that make the denominator zero are excluded.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Conic sections
knowledge.content: Conic sections are curves formed by slicing a cone. They include circles, ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas. Each can be described by an equation in two variables and has applications in orbits, optics and engineering.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Geometric transformations
knowledge.content: Geometric transformations move or change shapes. Translations slide, rotations turn, reflections flip and dilations resize. Rigid transformations preserve distances and angles, while dilations change size but preserve shape.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Bayes theorem
knowledge.content: Bayes theorem updates the probability of a hypothesis when new evidence is observed. It combines prior belief with the likelihood of the evidence under that hypothesis. Base rates matter, so a rare condition can still be unlikely after a positive test.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Sampling
knowledge.content: Sampling selects part of a population to learn about the whole. Random sampling helps reduce bias, while stratified sampling ensures groups are represented. Sample size affects precision, and how the sample is chosen affects reliability.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Hypothesis testing
knowledge.content: A hypothesis test uses sample data to assess a claim about a population. It compares evidence against a null hypothesis and reports a p value or similar measure. A statistically significant result is not automatically practically important.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Graph theory
knowledge.content: Graph theory studies networks of nodes and edges. It is used for roads, social connections, computer networks and dependencies. A path visits connected nodes, a cycle returns to its start, and a tree connects nodes without cycles.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Prime numbers
knowledge.content: A prime number is a whole number greater than one with exactly two factors: one and itself. Composite numbers have more than two factors. Prime factorisation expresses a number as a product of primes.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Modular arithmetic
knowledge.content: Modular arithmetic works with remainders. In modulo 12, 15 is equivalent to 3 because both leave remainder 3. It is used in clocks, calendars, cryptography and number theory.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Boolean algebra
knowledge.content: Boolean algebra works with true and false values. The main operations are AND, OR and NOT. It underlies digital circuits, search filters and logical conditions in programming.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Operating systems
knowledge.content: An operating system manages computer hardware and provides services for programs. It handles processes, memory, files, devices and user interfaces. Examples include Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: File systems
knowledge.content: A file system organises how data is stored and retrieved on a device. It uses directories, file names and metadata such as size and modification time. Permissions control who can read or change files.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Databases
knowledge.content: A database stores structured information for efficient retrieval and update. Relational databases use tables, rows and columns, while document databases store flexible records. Queries and indexes help find relevant data quickly.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Computer networks
knowledge.content: Computer networks connect devices so they can exchange data. Data is divided into packets that travel through routers and switches. Protocols define addressing, error handling and delivery rules.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Domain name system
knowledge.content: The domain name system translates human readable names like example.com into IP addresses. This lets people use memorable names while computers route data numerically. DNS records are cached to make lookups faster.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Cloud computing
knowledge.content: Cloud computing provides computing resources over a network on demand. Services can include storage, virtual machines, databases and software platforms. It can reduce upfront hardware costs but requires attention to security and pricing.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Encryption
knowledge.content: Encryption transforms data into a form that is hard to read without a key. It protects information in transit and at rest. Strong encryption depends on sound algorithms, secure keys and correct implementation.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Hashing
knowledge.content: A hash function maps data to a fixed size value called a hash. Cryptographic hashes are designed so small input changes produce very different outputs. They are used for integrity checks and password storage with added salt.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Phishing and security
knowledge.content: Phishing tries to trick people into revealing credentials or installing malware, often through convincing messages or fake websites. Check the sender, link destination and unexpected requests. Use multi factor authentication to reduce risk.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Version control
knowledge.content: Version control records changes to files so earlier states can be recovered and collaborators can work together. Git is a widely used distributed system. Commits, branches and merges organize development history.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Debugging
knowledge.content: Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors in software. A good approach is to reproduce the problem, form a hypothesis, test it and change one thing at a time. Logs, tests and small examples help isolate causes.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Software testing
knowledge.content: Software testing checks whether code behaves as expected. Unit tests examine small parts, integration tests check interactions, and end to end tests check complete workflows. Tests do not prove the absence of all bugs.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: APIs
knowledge.content: An API lets one program communicate with another through defined requests and responses. Web APIs often use HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT and DELETE. Clear documentation and stable interfaces make APIs easier to use.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
knowledge.content: HTML gives web pages structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds behaviour. These technologies work together in browsers. Semantic HTML improves accessibility and helps search tools understand content.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Data structures
knowledge.content: Data structures organise data for particular operations. Arrays provide indexed access, linked lists allow flexible insertion, stacks and queues control order, and trees and graphs model hierarchies and networks. Choosing well affects performance.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Neural networks
knowledge.content: Neural networks are models made of layers of simple computational units that learn weights from data. Training adjusts those weights to reduce prediction error. Deep networks can learn complex patterns but need sufficient data and care.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Overfitting
knowledge.content: Overfitting happens when a model learns noise or accidental patterns in training data and performs poorly on new data. Cross validation, more data, regularisation and simpler models can reduce it. Good training accuracy alone is not enough.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Tokenization and embeddings
knowledge.content: Tokenization splits text into units a model can process, such as words or subwords. Embeddings represent those units as vectors that capture learned relationships. Together they turn language into numerical inputs for a neural network.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Ancient Greece
knowledge.content: Ancient Greek city states developed distinctive political, artistic and philosophical traditions. Athens is known for democracy, philosophy and theatre, while Sparta emphasised military training. Greek ideas influenced later Roman, European and global culture.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Ancient Rome
knowledge.content: Ancient Rome grew from a city state into a vast empire. Roman contributions include law, engineering, roads, aqueducts and Latin literature. The western empire ended in 476, while the eastern empire continued as Byzantium.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Middle Ages
knowledge.content: The Middle Ages in Europe followed the fall of the western Roman Empire and preceded the Renaissance. Feudal landholding, castles, trade towns and religious institutions shaped society. The period saw both conflict and advances in farming, architecture and learning.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Industrial Revolution
knowledge.content: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 18th century and spread widely. Mechanised production, steam power, factories and new transport changed work and cities. It raised output but also created labour, housing and environmental problems.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: French Revolution
knowledge.content: The French Revolution began in 1789 and challenged monarchy, privilege and feudal structures in France. It produced declarations of rights, political upheaval and war. Its ideas influenced later movements while its violence remains debated.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Cold War
knowledge.content: The Cold War was a long period of political and military tension after World War II, centred on the United States and the Soviet Union. It involved alliances, proxy wars, espionage and an arms race. It ended with the Soviet collapse in 1991.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Civil rights movements
knowledge.content: Civil rights movements campaigned against discrimination and for equal treatment under law. The United States movement of the 1950s and 1960s challenged racial segregation and helped pass landmark legislation. Similar struggles occurred in many countries.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Forms of government
knowledge.content: Governments differ in who holds power and how leaders are chosen. Democracies select leaders through elections and protect political participation. Authoritarian systems concentrate power and limit opposition. Many countries use mixed or federal systems.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Constitutions
knowledge.content: A constitution sets out the basic rules, institutions and limits of government. It may define rights, powers, elections and the relationship between branches of state. Constitutions can be written in one document or developed across several sources.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Human rights
knowledge.content: Human rights are basic freedoms and protections that apply to people because they are human. Common examples include rights to life, education, fair trial and freedom of expression. Different legal systems protect them through constitutions, laws and treaties.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Ethics
knowledge.content: Ethics examines what actions are right, fair and responsible. Consequentialist approaches focus on outcomes, duty based approaches focus on obligations, and virtue ethics focuses on character. Real decisions often involve competing values and uncertainty.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Logical fallacies
knowledge.content: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that weakens an argument. Examples include attacking the person instead of the claim, assuming what should be proved and treating a rare dramatic case as typical. Naming a fallacy does not by itself prove the opposite claim.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Rhetoric
knowledge.content: Rhetoric is the art of persuasive communication. Classical appeals include ethos, which builds credibility; pathos, which appeals to emotion; and logos, which uses evidence and reasoning. Ethical rhetoric respects the audience and avoids deception.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Mythology
knowledge.content: Myths are traditional stories that explain origins, natural events, social customs or human behaviour. They often include gods, heroes and symbolic events. Different cultures have distinct mythologies, and the same story can have many versions.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Archaeology
knowledge.content: Archaeology studies past human societies through material remains such as tools, pottery, buildings and burials. Context is crucial because an object's location and associated finds affect its meaning. Ethical archaeology respects local communities and heritage laws.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Phonetics and phonology
knowledge.content: Phonetics studies how speech sounds are produced and heard. Phonology studies how sounds function in a particular language. A sound may be physically similar yet distinguish meaning in one language and not another.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Morphology
knowledge.content: Morphology studies the structure of words. A word can contain a root, prefixes and suffixes, such as un helpful ness. Morphemes are the smallest units of meaning in a language.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Semantics and pragmatics
knowledge.content: Semantics studies the meaning of words and sentences. Pragmatics studies how context changes meaning in use, such as sarcasm, implication and politeness. The same sentence can express different intentions in different situations.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Dialects
knowledge.content: A dialect is a variety of a language associated with a region or social group. Dialects can differ in vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation. They are systematic and rule governed, not faulty versions of a standard language.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Colour theory
knowledge.content: Colour theory studies how colours relate. Primary colours can be mixed to create secondary colours, while complementary colours sit opposite each other on a colour wheel. Artists use hue, saturation and value to create contrast and mood.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Visual composition
knowledge.content: Composition is the arrangement of elements within an image or design. Balance, contrast, rhythm, emphasis and unity help guide attention. Framing and negative space affect how a viewer reads the whole work.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Perspective drawing
knowledge.content: Perspective represents three dimensional space on a flat surface. Linear perspective uses converging lines and a horizon line to show depth. Atmospheric perspective uses lighter colour and reduced detail for distant objects.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Photography basics
knowledge.content: Photography controls light through aperture, shutter speed and sensitivity. A wide aperture lets in more light and reduces depth of field, while a fast shutter freezes motion. Composition and timing shape the final image.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Film basics
knowledge.content: Film combines images, sound, editing and narrative. A shot records a continuous view, a scene collects shots in one place and time, and editing controls pace and continuity. Camera angle and sound shape meaning.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Theatre basics
knowledge.content: Theatre is live performance in which actors, text, space and audience interact. Blocking is the planned movement of performers, while stage business is the small action that supports character. Live performance changes with each audience.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Architectural styles
knowledge.content: Architectural styles reflect materials, technology, climate and culture. Classical architecture uses columns and symmetry, Gothic architecture uses pointed arches and flying buttresses, and modern architecture often favours simple forms and open plans. Buildings can combine styles.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Typography
knowledge.content: Typography is the design and use of type. Typeface choice, size, spacing, line length and hierarchy affect readability and tone. Good typography helps readers scan and understand text without distraction.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Nutrition basics
knowledge.content: A balanced diet includes a variety of foods that provide energy, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre. Needs differ with age, activity and health. Nutrition advice should be adapted to individual circumstances and professional guidance when needed.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Exercise basics
knowledge.content: Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health, strength, mobility and mental wellbeing. A useful routine combines aerobic activity, strength work and flexibility. Increasing activity gradually reduces injury risk.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Sleep hygiene
knowledge.content: Sleep hygiene means habits that support regular, restorative sleep. A consistent schedule, a dark quiet room, limited late caffeine and reduced screens before bed can help. Persistent sleep problems should be discussed with a professional.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Hygiene basics
knowledge.content: Good hygiene reduces the spread of germs. Washing hands with soap, cleaning food surfaces, keeping wounds covered and staying home when seriously ill protect others. Hygiene practices vary with setting but share the goal of preventing infection.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Emergency preparedness
knowledge.content: Emergency preparedness means planning before disasters or accidents. Useful steps include keeping a contact list, storing water and basic supplies, knowing evacuation routes and learning local warning signals. Follow official instructions during an emergency.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Fire safety
knowledge.content: Fire safety includes smoke alarms, clear exits, safe cooking and careful use of electrical equipment. A small fire may be controlled with the correct extinguisher only if it is safe to do so. Otherwise, leave and call emergency services.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Road safety
knowledge.content: Road safety depends on obeying speed limits, wearing seat belts, avoiding impaired driving and staying attentive. Pedestrians and cyclists benefit from visibility and predictable behaviour. Local traffic laws should always be followed.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Digital wellbeing
knowledge.content: Digital wellbeing means using technology in ways that support health, relationships and work. Setting boundaries, taking breaks and curating notifications can reduce stress. Online privacy and security are part of healthy digital habits.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Note taking
knowledge.content: Effective notes capture ideas in your own words, not just copied text. Organising by headings, questions and key terms makes later review easier. Reviewing notes soon after learning improves retention.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Time management
knowledge.content: Time management starts with identifying priorities and estimating how long tasks require. Breaking large work into smaller steps reduces procrastination. Calendars, task lists and regular review help keep commitments visible.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Goal setting
knowledge.content: Specific and measurable goals are easier to pursue than vague wishes. A useful goal states the outcome, a deadline and a way to track progress. Reviewing obstacles allows the plan to change while the purpose stays clear.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Active listening
knowledge.content: Active listening means giving full attention, reflecting what you heard and asking clarifying questions. It helps reduce misunderstanding and shows respect. Avoid planning your reply while the other person is still speaking.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Public speaking
knowledge.content: Clear public speaking starts with a simple structure: opening, main points and conclusion. Knowing the audience, using short sentences and pausing at key moments improves clarity. Practice helps manage nerves.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Email etiquette
knowledge.content: A clear email states the purpose, needed action and relevant context early. Use a specific subject line, address the recipient correctly and proofread before sending. Match formality to the relationship and organisation.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Teamwork
knowledge.content: Effective teamwork combines clear roles, shared goals and open communication. Members should raise concerns early and record decisions. Respecting different strengths helps a group solve problems better than isolated work.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Conflict resolution
knowledge.content: Conflict resolution aims to address disagreement without damaging relationships. Start by stating the issue clearly, listening to each perspective and separating positions from interests. Agree on specific actions and follow up.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Investing basics
knowledge.content: Investing puts money into assets such as shares, bonds or funds with the aim of growth or income. Returns are not guaranteed and values can fall as well as rise. Diversification, time horizon and risk tolerance are important considerations.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Insurance basics
knowledge.content: Insurance transfers some financial risk to an insurer in exchange for premiums. Policies have limits, exclusions and deductibles that affect coverage. Reading the terms carefully matters before relying on a policy.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Consumer rights
knowledge.content: Consumer rights vary by country but often include protection from misleading claims, unsafe products and unfair contract terms. Keep receipts and written records when disputing a purchase. Consumer agencies can explain local options.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Gardening basics
knowledge.content: Successful gardening depends on climate, soil, light and water. Choosing plants suited to local conditions reduces effort and waste. Compost can improve soil structure, while mulch helps retain moisture and suppress weeds.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Recycling
knowledge.content: Recycling turns used materials into new products and can reduce demand for raw materials. Accepted items differ by local programme, so contamination from wrong items can cause problems. Reducing and reusing usually come before recycling in the waste hierarchy.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Energy conservation
knowledge.content: Energy conservation reduces use through behaviour and efficient equipment. Insulation, efficient lighting, sensible heating settings and turning off unused devices can lower demand. Small changes add up when applied consistently.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Weather safety
knowledge.content: Weather safety means preparing for hazards such as storms, heat, cold, floods and high winds. Official warnings should guide decisions. During severe weather, follow local advice and avoid unnecessary travel.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Home security
knowledge.content: Home security combines good locks, lighting, awareness and habits such as closing windows and not advertising absences. Alarms and cameras can help but should be used lawfully and with respect for privacy. Simple routines often matter most.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Travel planning
knowledge.content: Travel planning includes documents, transport, accommodation, budget, health needs and local customs. Copies of important documents and a backup payment method help when plans change. Check entry rules and safety advice before departure.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Transport safety
knowledge.content: Transport safety includes following vehicle rules, using appropriate restraints and staying alert as a passenger or pedestrian. Public transport has its own etiquette and safety guidance. Planning ahead reduces rushed decisions.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Ancient civilizations
knowledge.content: Early civilizations developed in river valleys where farming could support larger populations. Mesopotamia grew between the Tigris and Euphrates, ancient Egypt along the Nile, the Indus Valley on the Indian subcontinent, and ancient China along the Yellow River. These societies developed writing, law, trade, architecture and organized religion. Their achievements varied by region and time period.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: World wars
knowledge.content: World War I began in 1914 and ended in 1918. World War II began in 1939 and ended in 1945. Both conflicts involved many countries and caused enormous military and civilian losses. The wars reshaped borders, governments and international institutions. Historical explanations of their causes remain complex and are studied from political, economic and social perspectives.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Exploration and trade
knowledge.content: Long-distance trade connected regions long before modern transport. The Silk Road linked East Asia, Central Asia and the Mediterranean through networks of merchants. Maritime trade later connected Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas. Exploration expanded maps and exchange, but it also brought colonization, forced labour and disease. The consequences were different for each society involved.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Art movements
knowledge.content: Art movements are groups of artists who share ideas or styles. The Renaissance emphasized perspective, anatomy and classical subjects. Impressionism used loose brushwork and changing light. Cubism broke objects into geometric forms. Abstract art does not aim to represent the visible world directly. Movements overlap, and many artists work in more than one style.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Music theory basics
knowledge.content: Pitch describes how high or low a note sounds. A scale is an ordered set of pitches, and a key centres music around one note. Rhythm organizes sounds in time through beat and metre. Harmony studies how notes sound together, while melody is a sequence of pitches. Musical notation records these elements so performers can reproduce a piece.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Literature genres
knowledge.content: Fiction tells invented stories, while non-fiction presents factual accounts. A novel is a long work of prose fiction; a novella is shorter. Poetry often uses rhythm, imagery and compressed language. Drama is written for performance. A memoir recounts personal memories, and an essay explores a topic in prose. Genres can overlap and change over time.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Cooking basics
knowledge.content: Cooking applies heat to food to improve flavour, texture and safety. Boiling uses water at about 100 degrees Celsius at sea level. Frying uses oil at higher temperatures. Baking surrounds food with dry heat in an oven. Cutting ingredients to similar sizes helps them cook evenly. Food safety includes washing hands, avoiding cross-contamination and cooking foods to safe temperatures.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Personal budgeting
knowledge.content: A budget compares expected income with planned spending. Start by listing regular income, fixed costs such as rent, and variable costs such as food and transport. Subtracting total spending from income shows whether there is a surplus or shortfall. An emergency fund covers unexpected costs. Reviewing a budget regularly helps reveal patterns and support realistic goals.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: First aid basics
knowledge.content: First aid is immediate help given before professional medical care. Check that the scene is safe, call emergency services when needed, and avoid moving someone with a possible spinal injury unless they are in danger. For bleeding, apply firm direct pressure with a clean cloth. For burns, cool the area under cool running water. Formal first-aid training is the best way to learn these skills.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Home maintenance
knowledge.content: Regular maintenance prevents small problems from becoming expensive ones. Clean gutters, replace air filters, check smoke alarms and inspect seals around doors and windows. Turn off water and power before many repairs, and use the correct tools for the task. Electrical, gas and structural work should be handled by qualified professionals when required.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Language families
knowledge.content: A language family is a group of languages related by descent from a common ancestor. Indo-European includes English, Spanish, French, German, Hindi and many others. Sino-Tibetan includes Chinese languages and Tibetan. Afroasiatic includes Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic and the Berber languages. Language families are studied by comparing sounds, grammar and vocabulary.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Translation basics
knowledge.content: Translation carries meaning from one language into another. A literal word-for-word version can miss idiom, tone or cultural context. A good translator first understands the whole message, then chooses wording that sounds natural in the target language. Differences in grammar, politeness and references often require restructuring. Review by a fluent speaker improves accuracy.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Number systems
knowledge.content: Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on. Whole numbers add zero. Integers include negative whole numbers. A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers, such as 3/4 or -2/5. An irrational number cannot be written as a simple fraction, such as pi or the square root of 2. Rational and irrational numbers together form the real numbers. Complex numbers include a real part and an imaginary part based on i, where i squared equals -1.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Fractions
knowledge.content: A fraction has a numerator above the line and a denominator below it. The denominator tells how many equal parts make a whole. Fractions with the same value are equivalent, for example 1/2 and 2/4. To add or subtract fractions, use a common denominator: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. To multiply fractions, multiply numerators and denominators. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Decimals and percentages
knowledge.content: Decimal places show tenths, hundredths and thousandths. A percentage means a number out of 100. To find a percentage of a quantity, convert the percentage to a decimal and multiply: 25% of 80 is 0.25 times 80, which is 20. Percentage change is the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100. A 10% increase followed by a 10% decrease does not return to the original value.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Ratios and proportions
knowledge.content: A ratio compares two quantities, such as 2:3. A proportion says two ratios are equal, for example 2:3 = 4:6. Cross multiplication can solve proportions: if a/b = c/d then a times d equals b times c. Ratios are used for scales, maps, recipes and mixing quantities. Direct proportion means both quantities increase together; inverse proportion means one increases while the other decreases.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Exponents and roots
knowledge.content: An exponent shows repeated multiplication: 2^3 = 2 times 2 times 2 = 8. Any nonzero number to the power of zero is 1. Negative exponents mean reciprocals, so 2^-2 = 1/4. When multiplying powers with the same base, add exponents; when dividing, subtract exponents. A square root reverses squaring, so the square root of 9 is 3. A cube root reverses cubing, so the cube root of 8 is 2.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Order of operations
knowledge.content: Calculations follow a fixed order: parentheses first, then exponents, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. For example, 3 + 4 times 2^2 = 3 + 4 times 4 = 3 + 16 = 19. The same rules are sometimes called PEMDAS or BODMAS. Changing the order changes the result, so brackets should be used when a different order is intended.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Negative numbers
knowledge.content: Negative numbers lie to the left of zero on a number line. Adding a positive moves right; adding a negative moves left. Subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive. Multiplying or dividing two numbers with the same sign gives a positive result, while different signs give a negative result. For example, -3 + 5 = 2 and -4 times -2 = 8.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Linear equations
knowledge.content: A linear equation has an unknown with power one, such as 3x + 5 = 20. Solving means finding the value that makes the equation true. Do the same operation to both sides to keep the equation balanced. Here, subtract 5 to get 3x = 15, then divide by 3 to get x = 5. Always substitute the answer back into the original equation to check it.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Inequalities
knowledge.content: Inequalities use <, >, <= and >= instead of equality. They can be solved like equations, except that multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. For example, -2x > 6 becomes x < -3. Solutions can be shown on a number line with an open circle for strict inequality and a closed circle when equality is included.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Quadratic equations
knowledge.content: A quadratic equation has the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a not equal to zero. It can have two real solutions, one repeated solution or no real solutions. Some quadratics factor easily: x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 factors as (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3. The quadratic formula, x = (-b plus or minus the square root of b^2 - 4ac) divided by 2a, works for all quadratic equations.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Functions
knowledge.content: A function assigns exactly one output to each input. It is often written f(x), such as f(x) = 2x + 1, so f(3) = 7. The domain is the set of allowed inputs and the range is the set of possible outputs. A linear function has a constant rate of change and a straight-line graph. A quadratic function has an x squared term and a parabolic graph.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Coordinate graphing
knowledge.content: The coordinate plane uses a horizontal x axis and a vertical y axis. A point is written as an ordered pair (x, y). The slope of a line is the change in y divided by the change in x. For the points (2, 3) and (4, 7), the slope is (7 - 3) divided by (4 - 2), which is 2. The y intercept is where the line crosses the y axis, and the x intercept is where it crosses the x axis.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Pythagorean theorem
knowledge.content: In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a^2 + b^2 = c^2. If the legs are 3 and 4, then c^2 = 9 + 16 = 25, so the hypotenuse is 5. The theorem only applies to right triangles. It is used in construction, navigation, surveying and many coordinate geometry problems.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Circles
knowledge.content: The radius is the distance from the centre to the edge. The diameter is twice the radius. Circumference is the distance around the circle and equals 2 times pi times the radius. Area equals pi times the radius squared. For a circle with radius 3, the circumference is 6 pi and the area is 9 pi. Pi is approximately 3.14159.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Area and volume
knowledge.content: Area measures the size of a flat surface. A rectangle has area length times width. A triangle has area half of base times height. A parallelogram has area base times height. Volume measures space inside a solid: a rectangular prism has volume length times width times height, and a cylinder has volume pi times radius squared times height. Area uses square units and volume uses cubic units.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Angle rules
knowledge.content: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees and supplementary angles add to 180 degrees. Angles opposite each other at an intersection are equal. The interior angles of a triangle always add to 180 degrees. When a line crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal and alternate interior angles are equal. These rules help find missing angles in geometric figures.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Trigonometry basics
knowledge.content: Trigonometry relates angles to side lengths in right triangles. Sine is opposite side divided by hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent side divided by hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite side divided by adjacent side. Common exact values include sin 30 degrees = 1/2, cos 60 degrees = 1/2 and tan 45 degrees = 1. The Pythagorean identity sin^2(x) + cos^2(x) = 1 holds for every angle x.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Sequences and series
knowledge.content: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. In an arithmetic sequence, each term adds the same difference, such as 2, 5, 8, 11 with common difference 3. In a geometric sequence, each term multiplies by the same ratio, such as 3, 6, 12, 24 with common ratio 2. A series is the sum of sequence terms. The nth term of an arithmetic sequence is a + (n - 1)d.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Combinatorics
knowledge.content: Combinatorics counts arrangements and selections. A factorial n! is the product of all positive integers up to n, so 5! = 120. Permutations count arrangements where order matters, while combinations count selections where order does not matter. Choosing 2 items from 4 gives 6 combinations. The counting principle multiplies the number of choices at each independent step.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Set theory
knowledge.content: A set is a collection of distinct objects. The union of two sets contains everything in either set, while the intersection contains only what is in both. The complement contains everything in the universal set that is not in the given set. A subset has all its elements in a larger set. Venn diagrams show these relationships visually.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Logic and proofs
knowledge.content: A mathematical proof shows why a statement is always true. A direct proof starts from known facts and reaches the conclusion. A counterexample disproves a statement by giving one case where it fails. The converse of if A then B is if B then A, and it is not automatically true. The contrapositive, if not B then not A, has the same truth value as the original statement.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Calculus limits and derivatives
knowledge.content: A limit describes the value a function approaches as an input gets close to a point, even if the function is not defined there. A derivative measures an instantaneous rate of change and gives the slope of a tangent line. The power rule says the derivative of x^n is n times x^(n-1), so the derivative of x^2 is 2x. Derivatives are used for velocity, optimisation and curve sketching.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Calculus integrals
knowledge.content: An integral can represent accumulated quantity or the area under a curve. An indefinite integral finds a family of antiderivatives and includes a constant C, so the integral of 2x is x^2 + C. A definite integral gives a number between two bounds. The fundamental theorem of calculus connects differentiation and integration, showing they are inverse processes.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Statistical distributions
knowledge.content: The mean is the sum of values divided by the count, the median is the middle ordered value, and the mode is the most frequent value. The range is the largest value minus the smallest. Variance and standard deviation measure how spread out values are around the mean. A normal distribution is symmetric and bell shaped, with about 68 percent of values within one standard deviation of the mean. Correlation does not prove causation.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Financial mathematics
knowledge.content: Simple interest equals principal times rate times time. Compound interest adds interest to previous interest, so the amount grows faster. For example, 1000 at 5 percent compound interest for two years becomes 1102.50. Percentages are also used for discounts, tax, profit and loss. When comparing deals, calculate the final amount rather than trusting the advertised percentage alone.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Mathematical problem solving
knowledge.content: A reliable approach is to understand the question, list the known and unknown quantities, choose a strategy, calculate carefully and check whether the answer makes sense. Drawing a diagram or writing an equation often reveals the structure. Estimation can catch large errors before finalising an answer. If a direct method fails, try a simpler case, work backwards or look for a pattern.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Earth and the solar system
knowledge.content: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only known world with life. There are eight planets in the solar system. Earth has one natural satellite, the Moon. The Sun is a star that provides light and heat. Water covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface, and the planet has continents, oceans, mountains, rivers and an atmosphere.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Moon and tides
knowledge.content: The Moon orbits Earth about once a month. Its gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and helps cause tides. When the Moon and Sun pull together, tides are higher; when their pulls partly cancel, tides are lower. The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects sunlight.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Seasons and Earth's tilt
knowledge.content: Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees while the planet orbits the Sun. When a hemisphere leans toward the Sun, it receives more direct sunlight and has summer. When it leans away, it has winter. Seasons are not caused mainly by changes in distance from the Sun.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Stars and galaxies
knowledge.content: A star is a huge ball of hot gas that produces energy by nuclear fusion. The Sun is an ordinary star. A galaxy is a large system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Earth is in the Milky Way galaxy. Light from distant stars and galaxies can take many years to reach Earth.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Matter and its states
knowledge.content: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Common states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. A solid keeps its shape, a liquid takes the shape of its container, and a gas spreads to fill available space. Temperature and pressure can change a substance from one state to another, such as ice melting into water or water boiling into steam.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Energy and conservation
knowledge.content: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. It can appear as motion, heat, light, sound, electricity, chemical energy or stored position. The law of conservation of energy says energy is not created or destroyed in ordinary processes; it changes from one form to another. Machines and living things convert energy rather than make it from nothing.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Gravity
knowledge.content: Gravity is the attraction between objects that have mass. It gives objects weight, keeps people on Earth's surface, and holds planets in orbit around stars. More massive objects pull more strongly, and the pull gets weaker with distance. Gravity is not the same as magnetism, although both can act at a distance.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Atoms and elements
knowledge.content: An atom is the basic unit of a chemical element. It has a small nucleus containing protons and usually neutrons, surrounded by electrons. The number of protons determines the element. Elements are arranged in the periodic table by their properties and atomic number. Atoms can bond together to form molecules and compounds.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Light and sound
knowledge.content: Light is electromagnetic radiation that can travel through empty space. Sound is a vibration that needs a material such as air, water or solid matter to travel through. Light travels much faster than sound in air, which is why lightning is seen before its thunder is heard. White light can be split into a spectrum of colours.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Cells and life
knowledge.content: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out the processes of life. Some organisms, such as bacteria, have one cell. Plants and animals have many cells that form tissues and organs. Cells take in nutrients, release waste, respond to their surroundings and contain genetic instructions. Plant cells have cell walls and chloroplasts, while animal cells do not.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: DNA and inheritance
knowledge.content: DNA is the molecule that carries genetic instructions in living things. It is found mainly in chromosomes inside cell nuclei. A gene is a section of DNA that influences a trait. Offspring inherit DNA from their parents, which is why related organisms share features. DNA can be copied when cells divide, and changes in it are called mutations.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Photosynthesis
knowledge.content: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae and some bacteria use sunlight to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy. Oxygen is released as a by-product. The sugar stores chemical energy that plants can use for growth, and it forms the basis of many food chains.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Human body systems
knowledge.content: The human body has interacting systems. The circulatory system uses the heart to pump blood and move oxygen and nutrients. The respiratory system uses lungs to take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. The digestive system breaks food into nutrients. The nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord, processes information and coordinates responses.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Health basics
knowledge.content: Regular sleep, balanced nutrition, movement, hydration and social connection support health. Preventive care and vaccines can reduce the risk of some diseases. Health needs vary between people, and persistent symptoms should be discussed with a qualified health professional. Avoid sharing private medical details with untrusted systems.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Ecosystems and food chains
knowledge.content: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with each other and with their physical environment. Energy usually enters through sunlight captured by plants or other producers. Food chains show energy passing from producers to herbivores, then to predators and decomposers. Nutrients are recycled through soil, water and living things.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Arithmetic
knowledge.content: Arithmetic is the branch of mathematics concerned with numbers and the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Addition combines quantities, subtraction finds a difference, multiplication is repeated addition, and division splits a quantity into equal parts. Calculations follow an order of operations: parentheses, exponents, multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Algebra
knowledge.content: Algebra uses letters or symbols called variables to stand for unknown values or quantities that can change. An equation states that two expressions are equal. Solving an equation means finding values that make the statement true. Algebra is used to describe patterns, relationships and rules in science, engineering, finance and everyday problem solving.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Geometry
knowledge.content: Geometry studies shapes, sizes, angles, positions and space. A triangle has three sides and its interior angles add to 180 degrees. A square has four equal sides and four right angles. The area of a rectangle is length multiplied by width. The circumference of a circle is pi multiplied by its diameter, and its area is pi multiplied by the radius squared.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Probability and statistics
knowledge.content: Probability measures how likely an event is, expressed from 0, meaning impossible, to 1, meaning certain. Statistics collects, summarizes and interprets data. The mean is the average, the median is the middle value after ordering, and the mode is the most frequent value. Correlation between two things does not by itself prove that one causes the other.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Measurement and units
knowledge.content: A measurement needs a number and a unit. The International System of Units uses the metre for length, kilogram for mass, second for time, ampere for electric current, kelvin for temperature, mole for amount of substance and candela for light intensity. Prefixes change scale: kilo means one thousand, centi means one hundredth and milli means one thousandth.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Time and calendars
knowledge.content: A day is based on Earth's rotation, a month is loosely based on the Moon's cycle, and a year is based on Earth's orbit around the Sun. A week has seven days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. A common year has 365 days and a leap year has 366 days to keep the calendar aligned with the seasons. Time zones keep local clocks roughly matched to daylight.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Computers and binary
knowledge.content: Digital computers represent information using binary digits called bits, which have the values 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte. A processor follows instructions to perform arithmetic, move data and make decisions. Memory stores data being used now, while storage keeps data for later. Computer programs are sequences of instructions that tell hardware what to do.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Internet and web
knowledge.content: The internet is a global network of networks that uses protocols such as TCP and IP to move data between devices. The World Wide Web is a service on the internet made of pages linked by hyperlinks. Browsers request pages using HTTP or HTTPS and render HTML, CSS and JavaScript. HTTPS adds encryption so data between a browser and a site is protected in transit.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Algorithms
knowledge.content: An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of steps for solving a problem or completing a task. Examples include searching a list, sorting numbers and finding a route. A good algorithm is clear, terminates and produces the expected result for valid inputs. Algorithms differ in how much time and memory they need as the size of the input grows.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Programming languages
knowledge.content: A programming language is a formal language for writing instructions that a computer can carry out. Python, JavaScript, Java, C and Rust are widely used examples. Languages use variables, expressions, control flow and functions to organize logic. Compilers translate whole programs into lower-level code, while interpreters execute programs step by step.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Artificial intelligence and machine learning
knowledge.content: Artificial intelligence is the field of building systems that perform tasks usually associated with human intelligence, such as recognizing patterns, understanding language or making decisions. Machine learning is a branch of AI that improves a model's behaviour by adjusting parameters from training data. A trained model can generate or classify patterns, but training does not give it consciousness, feelings or guaranteed factual accuracy.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Data privacy and security
knowledge.content: Data privacy concerns what information is collected, why it is used and who can access it. Data security protects information with measures such as encryption, authentication, access control and backups. Strong unique passwords and two-factor authentication reduce account risk. Privacy settings and data exports help people understand and control what an application stores.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Critical thinking and evidence
knowledge.content: Critical thinking means examining claims before accepting them. Useful habits include separating observations from interpretations, checking whether evidence supports a conclusion, considering alternative explanations and noting the limits of a source. A confident tone is not evidence. When information is missing, it is better to ask a precise question or state uncertainty than to invent an answer.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Estimates and uncertainty
knowledge.content: An estimate is an approximate answer based on available information. An exact value usually requires a reliable measurement or source. Uncertainty should be stated when data is incomplete, noisy or changing. Ranges, confidence levels and assumptions make estimates more useful. An estimate should not be presented as a verified fact.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Clarifying questions
knowledge.content: A clarifying question helps when a request is ambiguous, uses an undefined term or lacks context. Good clarifying questions are short and target the missing information, such as which meaning, time period, place or goal is intended. Asking for clarification is a valid response when answering accurately would otherwise require guessing.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Learning and memory
knowledge.content: Learning is stronger when practice is spaced over time rather than crammed into one session. Retrieval practice, explaining an idea in your own words and testing yourself improve recall. Sleep helps consolidate memory. Mistakes are useful when they are reviewed and corrected, because the correction identifies what should change.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Cause and effect
knowledge.content: A cause produces or contributes to an effect. To judge causation, check whether the cause came before the effect, whether the two are related, and whether other explanations can be ruled out. Repeated association alone does not prove causation. Experiments and careful observation help separate genuine causes from coincidence.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Continents and oceans
knowledge.content: The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. The five oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans. Asia is the largest continent by area, and the Pacific is the largest ocean. Oceans regulate climate, provide food and contain a wide variety of life.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Weather and climate
knowledge.content: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions such as temperature, rain, wind and cloud cover. Climate is the long-term pattern of weather in a place, usually measured over decades. Weather can change from hour to hour, while climate changes much more slowly. Greenhouse gases affect climate by trapping some heat in Earth's atmosphere.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Maps and coordinates
knowledge.content: A map represents places using scale, symbols and a legend. Latitude lines run east and west and measure distance north or south of the equator. Longitude lines run north and south and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian. A location can be described with a latitude and longitude pair. Map scale relates distances on the map to real distances.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Money and trade
knowledge.content: Money serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. Trade allows people and countries to specialize in what they produce well and exchange for other goods and services. Prices are influenced by supply, demand, costs and expectations. Inflation means prices rise over time, reducing the purchasing power of a fixed amount of money.

knowledge.title: Knowledge: Rules and laws
knowledge.content: Rules are agreed expectations for behaviour in a group, while laws are rules made and enforced by a government or other authority. Laws differ between places and can change over time. They cover areas such as safety, property, contracts and rights. When legal guidance is needed, a qualified professional in the relevant jurisdiction should be consulted.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Basic English sentence structure
knowledge.content: English sentences use word order to show meaning. The basic parts are subject, verb and object. A subject is who or what acts. A verb is the action or state. An object receives the action. Articles such as a, an and the come before nouns. Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or whole sentences. Capitalize the first word of a sentence and use a full stop at the end.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Subject + Verb
knowledge.content: Pattern: Subject + Verb. Example: I run. Here I is the subject and run is the verb. This pattern needs no object.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Subject + Verb + Object
knowledge.content: Pattern: Subject + Verb + Object. Example: I read books. I is the subject, read is the verb and books is the object that receives the action.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Subject + Verb + Adjective
knowledge.content: Pattern: Subject + Verb + Adjective. Example: The sky is blue. The sky is the subject, is is the verb and blue is the adjective describing the sky.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Subject + Verb + Object + Additional information
knowledge.content: Pattern: Subject + Verb + Object + Additional information. Example: I learn English every day. I is the subject, learn is the verb, English is the object and every day tells when the action happens.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Nouns
knowledge.content: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. Examples: world, book, sky, English, friend. Nouns can be the subject or the object of a sentence.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Pronouns
knowledge.content: A pronoun stands in for a noun. I and we refer to the speaker. You refers to the listener. He, she, it and they refer to others. Example: I learn English. I is a pronoun acting as the subject.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Adjectives
knowledge.content: An adjective describes a noun. Examples: blue, careful, interesting. Example: The sky is blue. Blue describes the sky.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Adverbs
knowledge.content: An adverb adds detail to a verb, adjective or sentence. Many adverbs end in ly. Examples: carefully, quickly, every day. Example: I learn English every day. Every day tells when I learn.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Articles
knowledge.content: Articles are a, an and the. Use a and an for general things and the for a particular thing. Example: The book is on the table.

knowledge.title: Grammar: Punctuation and capitalization
knowledge.content: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and proper nouns such as English. Use a full stop for a statement, a question mark for a question and an exclamation mark for strong feeling. Use commas to separate items in a list.
